articles.title: Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win
articles.summary: White House counsel Will Scharf and his team are looking at 'what [Donald] Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in…

items: The Trump administration is preparing for a potential Democratic takeover of Congress by developing plans to advance its agenda through executive actions on issues like immigration and tariffs, while also bracing for investigations.

Senior officials are identifying legal avenues for Trump to act unilaterally, including changes to federal spending and grant rules, while Trump has expressed comfort with governing without congressional approval.

Democrats could face challenges in blocking Trump's actions, but they have the power to conduct investigations and could limit his judicial and executive nominations, while courts may also intervene against overreaching executive actions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON DC, USA – President Donald Trump‘s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.

Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at “what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court,” the White House official said.

The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday’s midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and constrain his spending priorities. But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call.
For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.
The White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.

“This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.
Federal agencies have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said.
Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said.

He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programs receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.
Trump has been briefed on the preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.
When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, “very comfortable.”

Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws.
A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.

“President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. “I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities.”

Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.
A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.
Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to block Trump’s judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme Court pick.

“I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president’s appointments,” said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.

Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he doesn’t like, and Democrats are unlikely to have enough votes in the House to override him.

Courts could block executive actions that exceed Trump’s legal authority. The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the people said.
One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations.

Reuters previously reported that senior House Democrats and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors.
Trump aides have been preparing for that prospect for months, all three people said.

White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency leaders on how to handle congressional inquiries, document requests and subpoenas, one person said. They have advised officials to be careful about what they put in writing.

They also sought a Justice Department opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, the person said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Welsh health board may close urgent primary care centres at three hospitals
articles.summary:
UPCCs in Holyhead, Tremadog and Bangor may shut as Betsi Cadwaladr University health board struggles with funding and recruitment

A struggling Welsh health board may close urgent primary…

blocks.text: A struggling Welsh health board may close urgent primary care centres at three hospitals, citing funding and recruitment issues, prompting widespread criticism.

Betsi Cadwaladr University health board, which serves about a quarter of Wales’s population, said it was consulting on ending urgent primary care centres (UPCCs) at Ysbyty Penrhos Stanley in Holyhead, Ysbyty Alltwen in Tremadog and Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor by April 2027.

UPCCs staffed by GPs, advanced nurse practitioners and physiotherapists – similar to urgent treatment centres in England – have been set up across Wales since 2020 to ease pressure on GP practices and emergency departments.
Local MPs and MSs from across the political spectrum have written to the board to warn of “dire consequences” – including additional strain on the services they were originally intended to help.

The Conservative MS Janet Finch-Saunders, who represents Bangor Conwy Môn, said: “These centres help to relieve pressure on our accident and emergency departments when people are unable to get an appointment with their GP but require immediate care.
“It is vital that [the health board] supports these centres to remain open. Without them, existing waiting times could increase, potentially leading to delays in treatment.”
Betsi Cadwaladr has been in special measures since 2015 due to concerns over care quality, patient safety and leadership. In June, it was given a “final chance” to improve.
The board’s chief executive, Carol Shillabeer, said in a statement that access to urgent and emergency care remained “a priority”.

The Welsh NHS has fallen behind the other UK nations in several key metrics despite significant funding increases. NHS spending takes up nearly half the Welsh government’s £27.5bn budget. Six of the country’s seven health boards were recently found to have failed in their statutory duty to break even over a three-year period as they struggle to control day-to-day costs.
after newsletter promotion

In September, Powys health board, which spans a quarter of the country, announced it was considering cutting 100 community hospital beds and consolidating minor injury services such as X-rays. Critics say the plans will make accessing care even more difficult for an ageing population in a rural region which is poorly served by public transport.

Opinion polls show that the NHS is overwhelmingly Welsh voters’ top concern. Turning the service around is widely seen as the most important of several fiscal challenges facing the new Plaid Cymru government elected in May.

articles.title: Spirit of 1676: remembering the Native American cataclysm of King Philip’s war
articles.summary:
The conflict that tore through New England 350 years ago was the bloodiest per capita in colonial or US history

Massachusetts is proud of its ties to the American Revolution. From Paul…

blocks.text: Massachusetts is proud of its ties to the American Revolution. From Paul Revere’s Ride to the siege of Boston, the past year-plus has been devoted to celebrating 250 years of US independence. Yet during this time, the state, and New England in general, has given far less attention to an older, more complex remembrance: The 350th anniversary of King Philip’s war.

King Philip, or Metacom, was an Indigenous leader from the Pokanoket people. Alarmed by English colonists’ infringement of Indigenous rights, from seizing land to proselytizing, Metacom led an alliance of New England tribes – including the Pokanoket, Nipmuc and Narragansett – in an existential struggle for control of the region. He gave his name to the conflict, but paid with his life – as did many others, soldiers and civilians alike. With an estimated 800 dead on the colonial side, and three to five thousand Indigenous slain, the war claimed more deaths per capita than any other in colonial American or US history.

For the Indigenous, the price of defeat was steep. The victorious English sold many into slavery, and executed others on Boston Common. The war marked a turning point in relations between the ascending colonial presence and an increasingly diminished Indigenous population, whose ancestors had met for a peaceful Thanksgiving celebration just a half-century before.

Today, the conflict continues to reverberate. With November marking both National Native American History Month and the Thanksgiving holiday, and 2026 marking 250 years of American independence, historians are reflecting on the impact of King Philip’s war, 350 years later – a somber moment amid the Revolutionary hoopla.

“Recognizing the two anniversaries occur at the same time offers a moment to reflect why some things get much more attention than others,” says Christine De Lucia, an assistant professor of history at Williams College in western Massachusetts and the author of the 2018 book Memory Lands: King Philip’s War and the Place of Violence in the Northeast.

Mack Scott III, an assistant professor of critical Native American and Indigenous studies at Brown University, and a member of the Narragansett tribe, says, “The way we remember it, when we do talk about it, is through ideas that become part of the lore of a nation, that we don’t even associate with the war but are definitely internalized as a community, as a people, as a nation: ‘This is the process by which the land becomes the US, and the process has some sort of benevolence.’

“A lot of people believed that,” Scott says, “[for them] it was an almost undeniable natural process, almost inevitable, it was going to happen in this way. They don’t remember how violent the war was for New England. That was the thinking about those processes – it was a promised land. When you frame it almost in those senses – it was almost inexorable, undeniable, natural, divine, supposed to happen – the removal of Indigenous people, the death of Indigenous people becomes almost preordained, natural, something you expect to see. Today, Native peoples are almost back-of-mind for most Americans.”
The situation was much different in 17th-century New England.

Metacom’s father, Massasoit or Ousamequin, held a powerful position as the leader, or sachem, of the Pokanoket. (The tribe has been connected to the Wampanoag people, although there is some dispute over this.) It was Ousamequin who helped the starving Pilgrims survive their first winter at Plymouth in 1620-21, and it was Ousamequin who joined in on that first Thanksgiving meal of coexistence. Yet the ensuing decades had altered the landscape. Pathogens brought by English and earlier European explorers had decimated the Indigenous population. A continual influx of English colonists tipped the population balance in favor of the newcomers, who increasingly encroached on Native land.

“It was like a pot that had been boiling for a long, long time,” says Brad Lopes, the education and public programs manager for the Aquinnah Cultural Center, and a member of the Aquinnah Wampanoag tribe on the island of Martha’s Vineyard. “Our ancestors faced almost an existential crisis … The world they knew, that our ancestors knew, would never really be around any more.”

Metacom’s older brother, Wamsutta, had been raised to succeed their father as sachem. Instead, shortly after assuming the role, Wamsutta mysteriously died after meeting with the colonists, with the less experienced Metacom becoming the new sachem. The colonists soon compelled Metacom to accept a humiliating agreement that incensed the Pokanoket.

Eric Schultz, co-author of the 2017 book King Philip’s War: The History and Legacy of America’s Forgotten Conflict, says that Metacom faced a “very complex moment”, one that “his father and brother never faced before”,
In June 1675, war erupted with an Indigenous attack on Swansea, in what is today south-eastern Massachusetts.

Metacom’s forces were “very successful at the outset”, says bestselling author Michael Tougias, who co-wrote King Philip’s War with Schultz. “They quickly adapted hit-and-run tactics into ambushes. The English were reeling. I often thought, had all the tribes in New England united, they would have pushed the English back into a ring around Boston.” However, he adds, “because so many natives did not join, ending up with the English or wavering on the side, it eventually tips the balance.”

When Metacom led a force into the colony of New York to seek an alliance with the powerful Mohawk tribe, it backfired: the Mohawk preferred fur trading with English colonists, and attacked Metacom’s men. Another powerful tribe, the Narragansett of Rhode Island, did join the conflict on Metacom’s side, but they lost heavily in an engagement remembered by the colonists as the Great Swamp Fight, and by Indigenous as the Great Swamp Massacre. Several tribes – the Mohegan and the Pequot – fought alongside colonists. Other Indigenous people, who had converted to Christianity and were called “Praying Indians”, sided with the colonists but their loyalty was doubted. Colonial authorities relocated them to Deer Island in Boston Harbor; there, running low on supplies in the winter, hundreds died.

Although Indigenous forces committed their share of depredations, they were unprepared for the scale of colonial vengeance, in engagements such as the Great Swamp Fight and the Turners Falls Massacre, or for the determination of the English to press the war at all seasons.

“This is a war of attrition,” says Donald “Strong Turtle” Brown Jr, the official historian of the Pokanoket and a descendant of Metacom. “Indigenous people cannot sustain their warriors or plant in the field. They surrender because they’re starving, or dying from exposure to the elements.”

One colonial military leader – Benjamin Church – successfully adopted Indigenous military tactics. When an Indigenous man named John Alderman offered to locate Metacom, Church listened. On 12 August 1676, Alderman guided an expedition to Metacom and killed the Pokanoket sachem at the tribe’s stronghold of Mount Hope in present-day Rhode Island.

Metacom’s head was displayed on a stake outside Plymouth. His wife and son were sold into slavery, as were many other Indigenous people. The conflict did not end in all of New England upon Metacom’s death; in Maine, the Wabanaki continued fighting until 1678 and, unlike many of their counterparts, they got to remain on their land.

“The issues that were present during King Philip’s War do not go away by the time of the American Revolution and the advent of independence in the US,” Williams professor De Lucia says. “In some ways, they intensify – the theft of Native lands, US attempts to diminish Native sovereignty.”

Recent decades have witnessed increasing interest in Indigenous history – consider the inclusion of Native Americans in the recent Ken Burns documentary on the Revolution, or the land acknowledgments now de rigueur at some US institutions. That’s what makes it difficult to understand the relative dearth of attention to King Philip’s war.

Amid the many Revolutionary 250th celebrations in Massachusetts, there have been some local, regional and inter-tribal commemorations of the earlier war. It is harder to find evidence of larger-scale events. The offices of the governors of three New England states involved in the conflict – Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island – did not respond to separate inquiries as to whether their state held, or is planning to hold, a commemorative event.

Three hundred and fifty years later, several federally recognized Indigenous communities remain in New England: the Wampanoag in Massachusetts, and the Narragansett in Rhode Island. Metacom’s community, the Pokanoket of south-eastern Massachusetts and eastern Rhode Island, have not received federal recognition. But they have been recognized by other entities in tangible ways.

“Because we remember who we are and celebrate our history, Brown University [in 2024] returned 255 acres of our ancestral land – Mount Hope in Bristol – to the Pokanoket tribe,” says Metacom’s descendant Brown. “It’s one of the largest land-back grants to a non-federally recognized tribal [community], so we can secure our ancestral lands in perpetuity.”

And, Brown says, “Rhode Island General Assembly Senate Resolution S1034 last year officially acknowledges the Pokanoket tribe as the ancient and ongoing stewards of our ancestral land. The past does not erase us. Our story continues.”

articles.title: Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union
articles.summary: Kazakhstan is struggling to deal with the legacy of the Soviet dictatorship. Some 85 years ago, Stalin deported hundreds of thousands of people: Some 400,000 ethnic Germans living in the USSR were…

image.caption: Soviet dictator Josef Stalin deported ethnic Germans from across the USSR to camps during World War IIImage: Volker Witting/DW

blocks.text: She wants to keep history alive. Yunna Kinereish, 22, is studying public relations in Kazakhstan's modern capital, Astana. She describes herself as a Kazakh German.
"I am German by ethnicity. But I also feel that I'm Kazakh, because I keep the traditions with my family, and I have this mentality," she told DW.
Kinereish, who belongs to the Wiedergeburt (Revival) Association of Germans in Kazakhstan, is one of 223,000 Kazakh Germans living in the Central Asian republic of Kazakhstan today.
Kinereish recently acted in a play at the association's youth theater that told the fate of her Russian German forebears.

blocks.caption: Yunna Kinereish is one of 223,000 Kazakh Germans living in Kazakhstan todayImage: Volker Witting/DW

blocks.text: From the 18th century onward, Germans were incentivized to leave Germany and settle in the Russian empire, including in Ukraine's Black Sea region.

But after the armies of Hitler's Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, Soviet dictator Josef Stalinstarted deporting hundreds of thousands of Germans living in Russia and Ukraine to Siberia and Kazakhstan.
Collective punishment
Innocent people who had nothing to do with Nazi Germany's invasion and atrocities were collectively held responsible by the Soviet power and denounced as spies and collaborators.
There were more than a million deportees, of whom at least 200,000 died as a result of expulsion, hunger, and forced labor.
"My family is part of this history, these terrible times. They were driven out of the Ukrainian village Kleinwärter, a settlement of ethnic Germans in Ukraine."

Yunna Kinereish says she was very moved by the personal stories she and her friends had brought to the stage at the House of Friendship, where the association has its office. "It's not easy for me, because it all touches my heart very deeply. I actually feel like crying. But when I'm on stage ..., I have to be strong."
Culture and remembrance under one roof

The modern-looking House of Friendship in the capital Astana is the center for German culture in the city. Financed primarily by the German government, it offers language courses, engages in social work and fosters a culture of remembrance, focusing on the themes of deportation and repression under the Soviet regime.

Yunna Kinereish doesn't only present the history of her people on stage: She is also documenting it on film. In 2025, she made a film about German women incarcerated in ALZhIR (Akmolinsk Camp for Wives of Traitors to the Motherland), among the most infamous in the Soviet Gulag system.

During Stalin's brutal campaign of political repression and state-sponsored terror in the 1930s, a period known as the Great Terror, the Soviet Union established its biggest camp system in Kazakhstan. 18,000 women passed through the ALZhIR camp alone. These women were imprisoned there only because their husbands had been convicted of being traitors or enemies of the people. Among them were 167 ethnic German women, whose stories are told in the film.
The memorial for the ALZhIR women's camp is located just outside the gates of Astana, which only became the capital in 1997.

Astana's roads are permanently clogged with traffic. There are almost no pedestrians, and no cyclists at all. The city is growing, with new buildings shooting up all along the outskirts of the city. Beyond them is the barren steppe; the village of Akmol is about an hour's drive away.

blocks.caption: The Arch of Grief is a huge steel construction that commemorates the suffering and forced labor the women enduredImage: Volker Witting/DW

blocks.text: Before entering the actual ALZhIR museum, the visitor passes through the Arch of Grief, a huge steel construction that commemorates the suffering and forced labor the women endured. The museum itself contains personal items that belonged to the female prisoners, models of their primitive quarters, original documents and photographs.
Representative stories

One of the photos is of Gertrud Platais, a woman with German roots who spent years incarcerated in ALZhIR. Platais was a print worker from Lower Silesia, part of modern-day Poland. She married Karl Eduard Platais and became a Soviet citizen. In 1938, during the Great Terror, her husband was arrested. Gertrud was convicted, too as a "relative of a traitor to the homeland."

She was transferred to ALZhIR, in a region where temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer and minus 40 degreees Celsius in winter. Here, she was forced to work as an embroiderer until 1946. After this, she was banished for life to the huge Karaganda Corrective Labor Camp, known as Karlag. Gertrud Platais wasn't rehabilitated until 1956. Hers is just one story documenting the terror of the Soviet system on Kazakh soil.

Karlag was by far the biggest camp system and its complex covered an area about 22 times the size of New York City. Karlag was not just a prison camp, but a huge economic and agricultural complex. Almost one million people passed through it between 1931 and 1959.
Around 10,000 prisoners are believed to have died here between 1940 and 1950 alone: of starvation, cold, sickness, and the effects of forced labor.

blocks.caption: Gertrud Platai was convicted as a "relative of a traitor to the homeland"Image: Volker Witting/DW

blocks.text: Staged remembrance

The museum sits in the middle of the Kazakh steppe, near the city of Karaganda, about 250 kilometers south of Astana. It is located in the building that used to house the camp system administration. Visiting German historians and specialists are slightly puzzled: People were not tortured or tormented in this building, it was simply where the administration was done.

Here, interrogation and torture cells have been reconstructed, and everything is underscored by melodramatic music pouring from ubiquitous loudspeakers. It comes across as staged rather than authentic. As at the ALZhIR memorial, the Karlag museum has few visitors. Even well-educated young Kazakhs probably don't know about it."

Many people in Kazakhstan, and certain areas of politics, have almost no interest in coming to terms with the country's often brutal history," says Katherine M. Erdman. An American anthropologist and archaeologist at the Nazarbayev University in Astana, she has been researching the Gulag system for about a decade now.
"The landscape has been shaped by forced labor"

"We wanted to find out where exactly the camps were, and how they can still be recognized today." Erdman and her students relied on modern technology such as drone flights, but conducting interviews and research on the ground was also a part of it.

"In many regions, the landscape has been shaped by forced labor," Erdman says. Factories were often constructed alongside the primitive living quarters. Houses were built using bricks made by forced laborers.

The researchers share their findings directly with neighbors and with local administrations. "Often we're just met with apathy, or flat-out rejection," says Erdman. At a time of economic and social advancement, many don't want to be reminded of the inglorious aspects of the past.

Erdman says there is a desire to demonstrate to the international community that the country is dealing with the dark side of its history, but that she often experiences lack of interest and even rejection. The academic has been conducting research in Kazakhstan for a decade, but there is no state funding for a further lectureship.

The Kazakh German Yunna Kinereish is one of the young people in Kazakhstan who want to ensure that the past is not forgotten. "My ancestors survived the Gulag system in Kazakhstan," she tells DW. "So it's important to me that we don't forget our roots, and that what our forefathers experienced and suffered is passed on."

This article, originally published in German, was written in the context of a study trip organized by the Federal Foundation for the Study of the Communist Dictatorship in Germany. Since 1998, the foundation, funded by the German taxpayer, has dedicated itself to studying and reappraising the former communist dictatorships in Germany, the GDR, and other countries.

articles.title: Biological weapons: The weaponization of disease
articles.summary: Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. But new developments in biotech and AI are a cause for concern. DW addresses some of the most important questions about their history,…

image.caption: Anthrax is one of the most dangerous biological agents: It has a high mortality rate and extremely resistant sporesImage: Heikki Saukkomaa/dpa/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence could potentially be misused to develop biological weapons. This may sound like science fiction, but scientists, security services, and international organizations are all looking at how to deal with this scenario.

Pathogens can be analyzed and altered with ever greater precision thanks to ongoing developments in biotechnology. Meanwhile, AI is able to evaluate vast quantities of data at astonishing speeds. As a result, experts are warning that, in the long term, modern technologies could also be misused to develop biological weapons.

Security services are concerned. In October 2026, Ken McCallum, head of the British domestic intelligence service MI5, warned that artificial intelligence could increase the risk from existing, or new, biological weapons – including from non-state actors.
Fine line between valid research and misuse

A report by the American AI company Anthropic in September 2026 highlights the topicality of the debate. Anthropic said it had identified and blocked numerous attempts to use its AI assistant Claude in connection with possible biological weapon research. The report said these attempts included grant applications for so-called "gain-of-function" research, as well as projects to research avian influenza variants that were potentially the most transmissible to mammals.

At the same time, Anthropic stressed that, although it could have a military application, such research could also relate to medical prevention. The difficulty in distinguishing between legitimate science and its possible misuse is one of the biggest problems in terms of the control of modern biotechnologies.
What are biological weapons?

Concerns about biological weapons are by no means new. Many pathogens — bacteria, viruses, fungi, and certain biological toxins — have the potential for weaponization. Familiar diseases include plague, smallpox, and botulinum toxin, but anthrax is one of the most notorious biological agents. Its resistant spores can survive a long time in the environment, and it has also been the focus of research by state biological weapons programs.
Melting ice brings new dangers

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs define a biological weapon as the targeted release of such biological substances for the purpose of injuring people, animals, or plants.

A biological weapon usually has two components: The biological substance itself, and a system for disseminating it. Experts refer to these as the "agent," such as a virus or bacterium, and the "delivery mechanism." Examples of the latter include missiles, spraying systems, and contaminated food.
Biological weapons belong to the so-called ABC weapons, alongside atomic (nuclear) and chemical weapons. They are often also counted as weapons of mass destruction.
How do they differ from chemical weapons?

Biological and chemical weapons differ in their mode of operation. Chemical weapons injure people through the toxic effects of chemical substances such as sarin or mustard gas. They will often take effect within minutes, or even seconds. Examples of the use of chemical weapons are the gas attacks in World War I, which involved chlorine gas, and later mustard gas; and the deployment of the nerve gas sarin in the Syrian civil war and by Saddam Hussein in Iraq.

Biological weapons, on the other hand, cause infectious disease. The effects become apparent only hours, days, or even weeks after they have been deployed. Some pathogens are also capable of spreading from person to person, meaning that the outcome is difficult to predict.

To summarize: Chemical weapons kill or injure through immediate toxicity, whereas biological weapons cause diseases. The possibility of human-to-human transmission makes the effect of a biological weapon particularly hard to calculate.
Are biological weapons subject to a worldwide ban?

Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. The first Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) came into force in 1975. This prohibits the development, stockpiling, acquisition, retention, production, and transfer of biological and toxin-based weapons.

The Convention, which has been ratified by 189 countries, can be seen as a development of the Geneva Protocol of 1925, which banned the use of biological weapons as a method of warfare. Only a few countries have not signed the agreement, or have signed but not ratified it, including Israel, Egypt, and Syria. All those who have acceded to the Convention have also committed themselves to destroying all stocks, production sites, and means of conveyance.

Chemical weapons are also internationally banned, but their control is seen as much more highly developed. The Chemical Weapons Convention is implemented by the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), which can carry out inspections and oversee the destruction of chemical weapons stocks.

There is still no comparable system for controlling biological weapons. States fear that inspection could expose sensitive research data pertaining to medicine, biotechnology, or the pharmaceutical industry. This is why the control of biological weapons relies to a great extent on transparency, voluntary reporting, and good faith.

One of the best-known examples of why the ban on biological weapons is insufficient on its own to prevent their use occurred in the United States in 2001. A few weeks after the attacks of September 11, several people received letters containing anthrax spores. 22 were infected, and five died.

blocks.caption: Million-dollar reward: In 2001, anthrax was sent by post to several prominent Americans in an act of domestic terrorismImage: USPS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why are biological weapons so hard to expose and control?

Finding biological weapons programs is much harder than controlling the production of nuclear or chemical weapons. Many technologies that could be used to develop biological weapons also have civilian applications. The same laboratory equipment used to develop vaccines and medicines could, in theory, also be used for military research.
Experts refer to this as the problem of dual use. Research can be done for peaceful medical purposes and, at the same time, have a military application.

Furthermore, a biological attack can initially look like a natural outbreak of disease. It is often only possible after extensive investigation to establish whether a pathogen was deliberately released or occurred naturally.

Perhaps that is also why biological weapons have been deployed at various times throughout history. Historical reports range from the poisoning of wells to catapulting the corpses of plague victims over the walls of a besieged town. The effectiveness of these methods is, however, disputed.
This article has been translated from German.

Hundreds of adult gaming centres in England have bingo licences that still qualify them for discounted business rates

Hundreds of high street “

blocks.text: Hundreds of high street “slot farms” could continue claiming a discount on their business rates, unless the government closes a loophole that allows them to pose as bingo halls.

John Healey singled out adult gaming centres (AGCs) in his first budget this week, in which he increased duty on slot machine takings from 20% to 25%, claiming he was “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.

As well as raising the duty, which will also affect bookmakers and casinos, he said AGCs and vape shops in England would no longer be eligible for a discount on business rates aimed at leisure and hospitality businesses.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been a vocal critic of AGCs and posted on Instagram after the budget to back the policy, a key plank of his pitch to improve British high streets.
However, many shops owned by the UK’s two largest slot farm companies, Merkur and Admiral, could escape the tax tweak, Guardian analysis suggests.

This is because they have obtained bingo licences for venues that appear to offer slot machines almost exclusively. Gambling Commission records suggest that hundreds of slot machine venues may have exploited this loophole.

blocks.caption: Many shops owned by the UK’s two largest slot farm companies, Merkur and Admiral, could escape the tax tweak. Photograph: allanbellimages/Alamy

blocks.text: When the Guardian visited four owned by Merkur and one owned by Admiral, all advertised bingo in their shop windows. However, the shops appeared to offer mainly slot machines inside. Bingo was available only on tablets stacked in one small corner of the room, allowing the venues to operate under a bingo licence.

In at least one case, captured in covert filming, a member of staff said nobody ever used the bingo tablets, and they appeared not to be in working order. The remainder of the venue was dedicated to slot machines offering a £2 spin every 2.5 seconds for a jackpot of £500. These category B3 machines are associated with higher levels of gambling-related harm than most other products, according to several studies.

One so-called bingo venue is the Merkur Slots shop in Stockport, where Wendy Hughes, who had terminal cancer, lost £2,000 over two spells lasting 16 hours. Merkur was fined £100,000 after the Guardian revealed the details of Merkur’s exploitation of Hughes, who has since died.

The Stockport branch of Merkur is among more than 200 arcades that are licensed as bingo venues, according to Gambling Commission records, despite appearing to be geared towards slot machine play. Some data is duplicated, making it hard to measure exact numbers.
Operators could also now convert their remaining AGC licences to bingo.

The Labour MP Alex Ballinger, a co-chair of the gambling reform all-party parliamentary group, welcomed the tax increase on slot machines but urged the government to be vigilant about the loophole. “We must ensure these licences cannot be used to sidestep the new business rates rules,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

He urged the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to proceed with proposals to tighten the licensing rules, amid a consultation. “The government has already recognised this problem, and I am confident ministers will work with the regulator to close loopholes and ensure enforcement going forward,” he said.

blocks.caption: The chancellor says he is ‘raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street’.  Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty Images

blocks.text: The business rates expert Paul Turner-Mitchell of the real estate intelligence company Altus Group said the outcome of the tax change could hinge on how the Treasury defined an AGC and how local councils chose to enforce the rules. “A bingo licence alone does not settle its business rates treatment,” he said.
Merkur and Admiral did not respond to a request for comment.
Joseph Cullis, the president of the arcade operators’ trade body Bacta, said the industry would be hit hard by the tax changes.

“My great-grandfather started our family business back in 1962, and we’ve spent more than 60 years building it into what it is today,” he said. “Like many of the family-run businesses I represent across the sector, this decision will force us to reconsider investment and make difficult decisions about our future. Even larger operators will now be forced to scale back their plans.”

articles.title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
articles.summary:
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.

The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.

But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.

blocks.caption: The port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.

The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.

Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.

By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.

China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.

blocks.caption: A girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026. Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/Reuters

blocks.text: It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.

Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.

China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.

One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.

blocks.caption: Workers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China. Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty Images

blocks.text: China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.

This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?

The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

articles.title: Chancellor fails to guarantee minimum wage pledge for younger workers
articles.summary:
Manifesto promise to equalise rates before next election is now ‘a question of when’, John Healey tells BBC

Labour looks less likely to meet its manifesto pledge to equalise the minimum wage…

blocks.text: Labour looks less likely to meet its manifesto pledge to equalise the minimum wage for younger workers before the next election, after the chancellor failed to guarantee the rise within that timeframe.

John Healey said on Sunday the government was still committed to the increase but failed to spell out when it would be achieved. In the budget, a rise in the minimum wage was handed to adults and under 20s, but there was no larger rise for younger workers, which would have been needed for a move towards equalisation.
Speaking on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, he said he would “take it one step at a time” amid fears that a rise could exacerbate youth unemployment.
Labour’s 2024 manifesto committed to closing the gap on pay for 18- to 20-year-olds. Last week’s budget saw a blanket increase of 3.9% for both bands.

Some senior MPs – including the housing secretary Angela Rayner while she was out of government – have previously expressed concern at the slow pace of the equalisation. In June, Rayner warned the government it must deliver on the promise.

blocks.caption: The chancellor told the BBC he would ‘continue to make trade-offs between jobs and wages’ amid fears about youth unemployment. Photograph: Jeff Overs/PA

blocks.text: Healey said on Sunday the government was still committed to the eventual equalisation.

“I legislated as a new MP for the national minimum wage when we first brought it in [in 1998], and so we’re going to have to continue to make those trade-offs between jobs and wages,” Healey said. But he denied Labour would break its manifesto commitment.

“There’s no question about whether or if. It’s a question of when. It’s a question of how fast. And I want to make sure that we can look hard at those trade-offs that inevitably are there between jobs and wages.

“I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation, a million youngsters written off, without any prospect of being helped into work and making a contribution to this country for the future.”
Healey also told the BBC he was prepared to keep the spending cuts – some more than 2% year-on-year – planned for before the next election in the last spending review.

Some thinktanks including the Institute for Fiscal Studies have criticised how the government’s deficit reduction plans seem predicated on making unpopular cuts that are unlikely to be enacted at a crucial electoral moment.
after newsletter promotion

“We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year,” Healey said. “But in the budget I also set out the ways that we’re preparing and the work we’ve got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions.”

Speaking on GB News on Sunday, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said the government would not make “crude cuts” to welfare to balance the books, because of the costs that would incur elsewhere.

“We will set out proposals in the new year, and then we will legislate to bring the welfare bill down in a fair and sustainable way, and according to our values as a Labour government. I know that other parties, such as the Conservatives and Reform, claim that they can do crude cuts to welfare,” she said.

“The Conservative government didn’t manage to do crude cuts because they know full well that if you push people into crisis, then you end up pushing costs into a different part of the public sector. So that’s not the right way to do it because, frankly, this isn’t realistic.
“The prime minister and the chancellor and the whole government is very clear that we do need to bring the welfare bill down, and we’re also not running away from difficult decisions.”

articles.title: Britain should not issue apology over slave trade, says Kemi Badenoch
articles.summary:
Tory leader says apology would be ‘navel-gazing distraction’ and would be used as lever for financial compensation

Kemi Badenoch has said an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic…

blocks.text: Kemi Badenoch has said an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.
Speaking to broadcasters on Sunday, Badenoch also questioned whether it was worth future leaders attending the Commonwealth summit, given that it was now dominated by calls for reparations.

The Conservative leader made the comments as Andy Burnham said he was considering a formal apology, before he flies to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda next week.

In an article for the Guardian, Burnham said there would not be reparations in the form of financial compensation, but said he was prepared to engage in helping poorer countries restructure debt on more favourable terms.

Badenoch said leaders should be “honest about the whole history, not select the parts that are politically convenient today, especially given Britain’s leading role in ending the transatlantic slave trade”.

“If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?” she wrote in a social media post.
Badenoch said Burnham’s apology was unnecessary because of comments made by Tony Blair two decades ago. “The Commonwealth should be looking forward, not endlessly backwards,” she posted.

Badenoch told Sky News she believed that even if an apology was offered, campaigners would see it as a step towards financial compensation. “What I’m worried about is that this Chogm summit is yet another opportunity for people to start asking Britain for money because of the slave trade. We need to start looking at how we can bring the Commonwealth together – start looking forwards, not backwards.

“I don’t think we should be giving any money to compensate people for the slave trade, and I don’t think that Andy Burnham needs to be apologising because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash.”
after newsletter promotion

Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the chancellor, John Healey, said it would be unfair for the British people to be hit financially for reparations when they had “no role” in the slave trade. “The prime minister has said, look, we are open to a discussion about an apology. He feels that that’s the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth leaders’ conference,” he said.

“But he doesn’t believe that reparations are the right approach, and considering a formal apology doesn’t mean accepting that British people now should accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago, in which they had no role.”

articles.title: Why ‘2 Valid IDs’ is on track to make PH film history
articles.summary: The movie about the Philippines' broken health system and bureaucracy may become country's top grossing indie social realist film

blocks.text: Super Entertainment Facebook
The movie about the Philippines' broken health system and bureaucracy may become country's top grossing indie social realist film

items: The independent film '2 Valid IDs' has grossed P80 million at the box office within its first 18 days, with expectations to surpass P100 million soon.
The film, which addresses social issues like bureaucracy and healthcare struggles in the Philippines, has received critical acclaim and won awards at the Cinemalaya festival.
Unlike typical indie films that focus on romance, '2 Valid IDs' resonates with audiences by portraying relatable everyday problems, highlighting the need for empathy and reform in the system.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Independent movie 2 Valid IDs is on track to make Philippine film history, as it recorded P80 million at the box office, the film’s director, Ma-an L. Asuncion-Dagñalan, disclosed on Sunday, November 1.

The film grossed P80 million in its first 18 days after opening in cinemas nationwide on October 14. It is expected to cross the P100-million mark this week. 2 Valid IDs was the top-grossing film in the 22nd edition of Cinemalaya last August, and Marietta Subong, more popularly known as “Pokwang,” won the festival’s Best Actress along with Ruby Ruiz (for Status: Rejected). 2 Valid IDs also got Cinemalaya’s Audience Choice Award (full-length film category).

blocks.caption: Why ‘2 Valid IDs’ is on track to make PH film history

blocks.text: And since the movie will likely extend for another week considering the strong support from moviegoers, 2 Valid IDs’ success at the box office is likely to continue.

“Nadagdagan pa tayo ng mga sinehan! ((We’ve got additional cinemas.) We are on our third week strong and still showing in 100 cinemas nationwide! Maraming maraming salamat, mga ka-#2 ValidIDs!” film outfit Super Entertainment, which has been promoting the film, posted on Sunday.

Ticket prices for 2 Valid IDs are P200 for a student/teacher; P275 for regular patrons in Metro Manila; and P230 for regular patrons in the provinces. Seniors get a 20% discount. Assuming a ticket price of P250, P80 million at the box office means that roughly 320,000 people have seen the film.

What makes 2 Valid IDs success unique is that it’s a social drama; most commercially successful indie films are love stories. It tells the story of Sylvia and her ailing farmer-husband, Ramon (played by Joey Marquez), and how red tape, corruption, and a broken health system fails a poor family.
Most cinema patrons don’t spend their hard-earned money for social realism, as movie-going is generally a form of escape.
The movie that holds the record at the box office is the 2017 romantic comedy, Kita-Kita, starring Alessandra de Rossi and Empoy, the love story of two migrant workers in Japan.

blocks.caption: Why ‘2 Valid IDs’ is on track to make PH film history

blocks.text: Kita-Kita started with a whimper at the box office, but ended with a bang as word of mouth about the movie spread. Kita-Kita earned a total of P320 million at the box office. Given a production cost of P10 million, the film gave a windfall to producers Piolo Pascual and Spring Films, and catapulted comedian Empoy’s acting career. Kita-Kita even got an Indonesian remake in 2017, Cinta Itu Buta (Love is Blind).

Unlike Kita-Kita, 2 Valid IDs is a drama that makes its viewers angry and frustrated over the Philippines’ broken hospital system and bureaucracy. The movie is more comparable to the second most successful indie film, Heneral Luna, than to Kita-Kita.

Starring John Arcilla and helmed by Jerrold Tarog, the 2015 surprise hit about the hot-tempered military general Antonio Luna during the Philippine-American war, is the country’s highest grossing historical indie film. It earned around P250 million, allowing it to break even given producer Artikulo Uno’s high budget of P240 million. The film resonated with lines that evoke patriotism, including,“Negosyo o kalayaan? Bayan o sarili? Pumili ka.” (Business or freedom? Country or self-interest? You choose.)

blocks.caption: Why ‘2 Valid IDs’ is on track to make PH film history

blocks.text: Most indie films don’t last a week in theaters, especially now with streaming platforms becoming the preferred platform for watching films and other entertainment content.
Critics and analysts have lauded the film for portraying an issue that resonates among Filipinos: the difficulties often encountered when they deal with most front-line government agencies.

“The film is a searing ethnography of cascading exclusion. Each door that closes on Sylvia also closes the next. Without an ID, she cannot claim money that is already hers. Without the money, her husband cannot be moved up for surgery,” said UP professor emeritus and political analyst Randy David in a recent column.

Edielyn Mangol, writing for People, Places, Plates, said: “Films tackling poverty, bureaucracy and access to public services can sometimes be perceived as difficult or niche compared with mainstream commercial releases. 2 Valid IDs is showing that a story rooted in an everyday Filipino problem can still attract paying audiences when it is told in a way that feels personal and relatable.”

Asuncion-Dagñalan, in a film director’s statement on Cinemalaya: “It’s only in the Philippines that we are asked to show 2 valid IDs to get another ID. What happens to those who don’t have any? What happens to the people trapped in a chaotic and inhumane system?

“2 Valid IDs is more than a story of bureaucracy, it is a reflection of the truth where access to basic needs is hindered by poverty, excessive red tape, rigid rules, and a system that demands documentation rather than urgency and compassion. Hence, many Filipinos are pushed into a world of ‘fixers’, forged identities, and moral compromise. They are doing this not because of selfishness, but out of necessity and love….

“Ultimately, the film 2 Valid IDs is a cry for empathy, reform, and a more humane way of treating the most vulnerable. It’s a film that calls us to look at our institutions and ourselves with a greater kindness, some added sensitivity, and more humane concern.”

The movie’s popularity prompted Akbayan Representative Chel Diokno to remind the public that only the National ID is needed for transactions with the government and private companies under Philippine laws, and requiring other IDs can penalized by up to P500,000.

“Sa ilalim ng PhilSys Act (RA 11055) at Executive Order No. 162, opisyal at sapat na patunay ang National ID sa anumang transaksyon sa gobyerno man o sa bangko at pribadong kompanya. Ang sinumang tumanggi rito nang walang valid na dahilan ay pwedeng magmulta ng hanggang P500,000,” he said in a social media post following the film’s surprise at the box office.

After the film crossed P50 million in ticket sales last week, its producer reminded the public to vote wisely in the elections: “P.S. Sana ay pagdating ng botohan ay makapag-desisyon tayo para mabago ang sistemang nagpapahirap sa mga Pilipino.”
(Hopefully, when we vote, we are able to decide to change the system that impoverishes the Filipino.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Portugal police storm housing protest camps in Lisbon, Porto
articles.summary: Clashes broke out as officers again dispersed housing protesters from tent camps in Lisbon and Porto. Portuguese police have repeatedly cleared tent camps erected across both cities in recent weeks.

image.caption: Protests over soaring housing costs have intensified in Portugal in recent weeksImage: Filipe Amorim/AFP

blocks.text: Police on Sunday cleared out protest camps in Portugal's capital, Lisbon, and Porto after thousands of housing protesters marched against a rental bill.

Around 4:30 a.m. local time (0430 GMT), ‌dozens of officers moved in to dismantle camps in Lisbon's Rossio Square and Porto's Dom Joao I Square, where participants had set up tents following peaceful marches against soaring housing costs on Saturday.
Police used shields and batons to disperse protesters, and said some of the demonstrators threw bottles and paint at officers as they stormed the camps.

blocks.caption: Dozens were reportedly injured after riot police clashed with housing protestersImage: Filipe Amorim/AFP

blocks.text: Police arrest 13 in Lisbon, Porto

Six people were arrested in Lisbon and seven in Porto for refusing orders to disperse, according to a police statement. It said 13 police were injured as they tried to take down the camps, with eight taken to hospital.
The statement also said an unspecified number of civilians were also injured.
Meanwhile, one of the lawyers representing those detained in Porto said the police response was disproportionate, arguing that both the size of the operation and the actions were excessive.
Activist group Acampada Lisboa said more than 30 protesters were injured, including 10 who required hospital treatment.
It called a fresh rally against the police operation in the capital on Sunday afternoon. "We will not be silenced," the group said in a statement posted on social media.
Portugal's housing crisis
Hours before the eviction, more than 1,000 people marched through central Lisbon to protest against Portugal's deepening housing crisis.
Demonstrators are calling for the country's minority center-right government to scrap plans that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases.
Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has ruled out withdrawing the bill, though he has acknowledged that modifications could be made before the final vote.
Portugal is facing one of Europe's most severe housing crises, with house prices more than doubling since 2017.

articles.title: In wake of Wainwright tragedy, this year's Silver Cross Mother has a message for grieving families
articles.summary: Virginia Hicks is this year's national Silver Cross Mother, an annual tradition by the Royal Canadian Legion recognizing the mother of a fallen Canadian Armed Forces member each Remembrance Day.…

image.caption: National Silver Cross Mother Virginia Hicks stands by the grave of her daughter Sapper Mariebeth Short. A combat engineer preparing for a possible deployment to Afghanistan or Bosnia, Short was killed during a training exercise at CFB Petawawa in 2002. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)

blocks.text: Every year, Virginia Hicks visits Canadian Forces Base Petawawa in northern Ontario. That's where her daughter Sapper Mariebeth Short was killed during a training exercise on Sept. 23, 2002.
Sapper Short enrolled in the Canadian Armed Forces in 2000, eventually landing at 2CER, a combat engineering regiment, at CFB Petawawa in 2001.
"She was a go-getter. She never stopped, she never quit," Hicks said.
Sapper Short was preparing for a possible deployment to Afghanistan or Bosnia. She was 22 years old when she died.
Virginia Hicks is this year's national Silver Cross Mother, an annual tradition by the Royal Canadian Legion recognizing the mother of a fallen Canadian Armed Forces member each Remembrance Day.
The 4’11” combat engineer who proved everyone wrong
"It's a club nobody wants to belong to," Hicks told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault from her home in Frankford, Ont. "In order to receive one, someone you love had to have died."
Short was killed when the light armoured vehicle (LAV) she was in rolled over during a training exercise.
Hicks' annual visit to CFB Petawawa with her husband Brian has become one way for the family to honour her daughter's time in service.
Sapper Mariebeth Short was killed in a LAV rollover on CFB Petawawa in 2002. (Virginia Hicks)
At the crash site, a small bush in 2002 has grown to stand many feet above Hicks' head.
"I think her pride in her job has kind of fallen back on us. I know that she's passed, she's in a better place."
'Never going to be forgotten'
As the Silver Cross Mother, Hicks will lay a wreath at the cenotaph in Ottawa during the national ceremony on Nov. 11.

items: 'Quiet, independent, strong-willed': B.C. soldier burned at CFB Wainwright faces long recovery, family says
Police, military escort body of fallen Wainwright soldier through Calgary

blocks.text: This year's Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa will also be taking place a few weeks after a deadly grass fire swept through a training area at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Four soldiers were killed, and dozens more were seriously injured on Oct. 17.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, lost their lives and are being mourned across the country. A military investigation into the training accident is underway.

This composite image shows the soldiers who died following a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. From left: Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark and Sgt. Morgan Wong. (Canadian Armed Forces/The Canadian Press)
Hicks remembers when she first heard about what happened in Wainwright.
"We were sitting on the couch and all of a sudden it was just like you had a cold shower. I was like, oh my God, not again," Hicks recalled.
"I said, well, I now have four more members of our club."
Silver Cross Mother urges CFB Wainwright families to ‘have faith’
Hicks empathizes with the families of those who died at CFB Wainwright. They will now also be awarded a Memorial Cross, a decoration given to those whose loved one died in service.

"I'm hoping that other Memorial Cross recipients understand that there is support. There's people out there that can help you with whatever you want, and your child or your husband or your wife are never going to be forgotten because their name is written down in history."
Hicks also encouraged the families to "have faith" in the military's investigation.
Small but mighty
Sapper Short's nickname on base was "Shorty."
"She was 4-foot-11, 90 to 95 pounds, and she was a combat engineer, so her job was big and heavy," said Hicks.
“She was small in stature ... but mighty, very mighty."
Hicks says Sapper Short's size was no deterrent to her decision to become a combat engineer.
"Her job was digging up mines, building bridges, driving LAVs, … knowing how to put a bridge together, carrying a bridge pin (weighs about 35 to 40 pounds) and she used to carry two."
Hicks had spoken to her daughter just days before the training was to begin.
“She said, I've been looking forward to this (exercise) for weeks. And I said, OK, we'll speak Friday when you're all done with your exercise. And that was the last time I spoke with her."
Hicks stands by her daughter Sapper Short's grave in Trenton, Ont. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)
Sapper Short was a fourth-generation member of the military. Her grandfather and great grandfather served.
Her mother, Virginia Hicks, served 29 years in the Forces, becoming a sergeant, with deployments to the Persian Gulf, Golan Heights, Kabul, Kandahar and Italy.
Her stepfather Brian Hicks was also a construction engineer who served 30 years.
Still, Hicks was a little surprised when Short said she wanted to join the military shortly after graduating high school.
Sapper Mariebeth Short was killed during a LAV rollover on CFB Petawawa in 2002. (Submitted by Hicks Family)

"Mariebeth was quite a different kid … but she was a sweetheart,” Hicks said. Short went through a goth phase in high school, then tried working in retail and fruit picking before settling on a career in the military.
Short was sworn in January 2000, doing her CER training at CFB Gagetown in southwestern New Brunswick, before being posted at CFB Petawawa.
"She was proud as punch," Hicks recalled. "She goes, this is where I want to be."
But Hicks admits dealing with the grief of losing her daughter made her almost want to quit the service.
"We came very close to pulling the pin … after the accident. And it took us a couple of years, I think, to put ourselves together and say, OK, we're gonna stay."
Now, as Hicks prepares for this year's Remembrance Day ceremony, she is remembering all those who have lost someone.
"For me, it's a way of showing my pride to my country and to my daughter, for the sacrifices that she did for her own country."

blocks.text: November 1, 2026
German Gen Z group calls for more demonstrations

blocks.caption: Gen Z regelt called on people to take to the streets again on November 14 for more demonstrationsImage: Uli Deck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The group that organized this weekend's protests, "Gen Z regelt" roughly "Gen Z takes charge," distanced itself from violent riots that occurred after the rallies and called for new demonstrations later this month.
The initiative's organizers issued a positive assessment of protests across Germany.
"Today, 100,000 people showed why they're taking to the streets," a spokesperson for the initiative said Saturday, adding that estimates of participation in six to eight cities would come later.

blocks.caption: At a rally in Münster, protesters held signs calling for money for education and universitiesImage: David Ebener/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gen Z regelt planned protests in 34 cities, including Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and Munich, and has called for people to take to the streets again on November 14.

The group has called for more funding for schools, addiction treatment, and psychotherapy as well as measures to combat rising living costs. While it promotes social justice and greater climate protection, it opposes the introduction of mandatory military service, as well as an expansion of government surveillance.

"We are here ‌today ​to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion," Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said Saturday in Berlin. "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden."
Gen Z regelt distanced itself from the violent riots and looting that followed the protests in some cities.
"We did not have any influence on what happened after the demonstrations," the group's spokesperson said.
Police also confirmed the demonstrations themselves were largely peaceful and that looting and riots afterward were set off by extremists using the protests for cover.

"The Gen Z protests turned out to be very peaceful," Andreas Rosskopf, chairman of the police union representing the Federal Police, told the Rheinische Post. He added that the groups responsible for the violence consisted of "autonomous and, in some cases, masked individuals."
In Cologne, which also saw looting, a police spokeswoman said the incidents were more likely linked to Halloween celebrations than to the aftermath of the Gen Z protests.

WASHINGTON DC, USA – The top Democratic lawmakers on the congressional intelligence committees on Wednesday, October 21, said they received an intelligence briefing that Russia has been waging a misinformation campaign against Democrats running in next month’s midterm elections.

The comments by Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes come as Republican President Donald Trump has in recent weeks eased economic sanctions on Russia and increased pressure on Ukraine to end its fight against Russian forces.

Warner and Himes told reporters they were limited in revealing what they had learned in an election security briefing that they had requested from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton because it was classified.
But, they said, Russia was waging the same kind of online misinformation campaign that the US intelligence community had tracked in US elections in 2016, 2020, and 2024.
“And the state of play, I would argue, is that, you know, Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats,” Warner said.

He noted news reports that Democrat James Talarico, who is running for the US Senate in Texas, and Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election in Georgia, “in particular are being dinged” by fake advertisements created with AI.
The White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Moscow in the past has denied meddling in US elections.

blocks.caption: Twitter, Facebook flag Trump posts, battle spills to social media

blocks.text: Himes said the pair could not provide details of the misinformation spread by Russia because the material was classified. But he added that Moscow’s conduct has been “the same old, same old.”
“The Russians are kind of throwing everything out there,” said Himes. “Chaos, you know, don’t trust your voting machines.”
He added there was “no reason to believe” that China has not been conducting “extremely targeted” efforts as it has done in the past to influence voters.

Beijing has previously denied interfering in US elections and the Chinese Embassy in Washington on Wednesday described Himes’ comment as “a false allegation and serious smear that has long been proved to be unfounded.”

Recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has shown Democrats leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by high single digits to low double digits nationally, bolstering Democratic hopes of regaining control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate.
The lawmakers said they were concerned that Trump could pursue efforts to contest election results, including by claiming foreign hacking of voting infrastructure.
Himes emphasized that there was no evidence that any country could penetrate US election systems and change results.
“Nothing out there suggests that there is even the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment,” said Himes. – Rappler.com
