articles.title: Alberta woman accused of sex with 15-year-old guilty of sexual assault
articles.summary: Jurors have reached a verdict in Alexa Suitor's sexual assault trial, finding Suitor guilty of sexual assault and sexual interference.

image.caption: Jurors returned a guilty verdict Saturday in the sexual assault trial of 35-year-old Alexa Suitor. (Facebook)

blocks.text: Calgary·Breaking
Jurors have reached a verdict in Alexa Suitor's sexual assault trial, finding Suitor guilty of sexual assault and sexual interference.
Jurors returned verdict Saturday afternoon after deliberating since Friday afternoon
A Sundre, Alta. woman accused of having sex with a 15-year-old boy at a New Year's Eve party has been convicted of sexual assault and sexual interference.
Alexa Suitor, 35, did not outwardly react when the jury foreperson read the verdict Saturday afternoon after 24 hours of deliberating.
The jury began deliberations Friday afternoon after hearing closing arguments prepared by prosecutors James Molloy and Laura Somers and defence lawyer Patrick Fagan.
Justice Douglas Mah will hear sentencing arguments at a later date.
Fagan indicated to the court he will be asking for a discharge for his client, which would mean she would not serve any time in jail.

items: 'We did not have sex': Sundre woman accused of sexually assaulting teen boy testifies in own defence

blocks.text: Over the week-long trial, the jury heard that on Dec. 31, 2023, a number of teens and adults attended a New Year's Eve party at a home in the Sundre area.
The teens and Suitor spent most of the night drinking in a cabin on the property while the other adults hung out in the main house.
'We took it too far'
At the end of the night, Suitor and several of the teens worked out sleeping arrangements. Some were to spend the night on cots in the living room; others would be in the bedrooms.

The victim — who CBC News is calling C.D. to comply with a publication ban — testified that he fell asleep on a cot and woke up to Suitor touching his penis. He said this led to sexual intercourse on the cot.
C.B. said the next day, he received a Snapchat message from Suitor saying “we took it too far last night.”
Two friends of C.B.’s also testified.
Suitor denied sexual touching
One friend said that she saw the pair having sex when she went into the kitchen to get a glass of water.
The other friend said that he saw the next-day Snapchat message from Suitor.
Suitor testified in her own defence, telling jurors that the sex and sexual touching never happened.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: NASA telescope predicted to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission
articles.summary: An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.

image.caption: In this image provided by NASA, Spectrum Astro workers remove the final pieces of protective cover on the Swift spacecraft in Hangar AE at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Fla., in September 2002. (NASA/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.
Years of intense solar activity dragged Swift down faster than usual
The U.S. Space Force predicts the Swift Observatory will come crashing down on or around Friday.

Most of the 1.5-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive re-entry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist.

Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the re-entry zone. The Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.

Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning yet full of gratitude for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma ray bursts and supernovas.
Workers look at the final pieces of protective cover on the Swift spacecraft that must be removed at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in September 2002. (NASA/The Associated Press)

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.

Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company's three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 12 to 15 kilometres to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.

items: This satellite is falling towards Earth, so scientists hatched a plan to give it a lil' push

blocks.text: Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma ray bursts and other ultra high-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope's superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.
"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek said in an email.

articles.title: Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter dismissed with prejudice
articles.summary: A federal judge on Saturday threw out U.S. President Donald Trump's multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump listens at a campaign rally at the Ocean Center, in Daytona Beach, Fla., on Friday. On Saturday a federal judge dismissed Trump's multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on Trump's relationship with

blocks.text: World·Breaking

A federal judge on Saturday threw out U.S. President Donald Trump's multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Judge finds U.S. president did not prove defendants made statements with actual malice
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice.

The lawsuit was over a story the Journal published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.
More to come.

articles.title: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
articles.summary: After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the eleciton losers still hold sway in the judiciary and…

image.caption: Supporters of the Student List celebrate victory on election night in Belgrade: The party gained an absolute majorityImage: Marko Djurica/REUTERS

blocks.text: Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."
Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.
Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."
Old accusations against Vucic

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

blocks.caption: Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat in the parliamentary elections on October 25Image: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.
Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.
How much damage can the old government do to the new one?

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."
Against all odds: How Serbia's students took on Vucic

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.
No change in foreign policy

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Clashes erupt between police and protesters in Paris
articles.summary: Over 320,000 people protested around France in a third weekend of demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services.

blocks.text: Police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters on the outskirts of Paris in a third weekend of nationwide demonstration against the rising cost of living and poor public services.
Over 320,000 people took to the streets around the country and at least 290 protesters were arrested, according to France's interior ministry.
Police say about 70,000 participated in the demonstration in Paris.
The authorities prepared extensively to avoid a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that happened two weeks ago.

articles.title: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied frontline city
articles.summary: One evacuated couple says they crossed minefields in Oleshky in a search for food.

items: Warning: This story contains graphic content.

blocks.text: Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the frontline city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".
Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."

The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.
Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.

Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.

As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.
Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.
"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.

That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.
Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.
Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on busses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday.
On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers. Others experienced emotional reunions.

Tetiana and Volodymyr, a couple carrying a cat when they arrived in Chernihiv, said their entire home was burned down three years ago, and they had been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour since.

For them, leaving as soon as it was safe to do so was an easy decision. "There's nothing for us to regret leaving. We don't have relatives there. Our children are married and don't live with us in the city," said Tetiana.
But those who managed to escape also worry about those left behind. "There are still a lot of people left there, living under those conditions," said Olha.
Now that the evacuees have left Oleshky, they will also face a new challenge - working out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.
Palii said he would look for a job so he can provide for his family: "There's no job I can't handle. Digging, hoeing, planting, building. I can even do demolition work."
Olha said she and her family have no relatives elsewhere in Ukraine, and they will stay with some acquaintances for an extended period while they get back on their feet.
She said: "If we managed to survive in hell, we'll survive here too."

articles.title: Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposal
articles.summary:
Inner west Sydney seat has long been safely held by the PM – but potential changes to copyright laws are angering its large creative community

  • Get our

blocks.text: The prime minister is facing growing discontent within his own electorate as creatives push back against the federal government’s proposal to allow AI companies to scrape everything Australians create online.

Anthony Albanese’s seat of Grayndler in Sydney’s inner west is home to more than 3,000 cultural and creative businesses, and 10% of its workers are employed in cultural and creative fields – compared with 4.2% nationally.
He has held it on a safe margin for three decades, and has spoken of its high representation of live music, theatre and artist spaces with pride.
But now, as Labor considers giving AI companies unrestricted access to Australian creatives’ works by default as it pursues a compromise with US tech giants, locals are reacting with dismay.

Labor is mulling over the copyright changes in a suite of reforms surrounding AI, including datacentres, energy and the economy. While Albanese has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train their models using Australian material.

Some AI companies have said making licensing agreements under existing copyright law would be too difficult, while Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder objected, prompting warnings from Coalition senators and the recording industry that this could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.
The federal government’s draft laws are expected by the end of the year, with consideration in parliament due in 2027.

blocks.caption: Pete Strong says AI is ‘the wild west and we really need to push back’. Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian

blocks.text: Pete Strong is a screenprinter and Greens councillor for Bayside. His business is based in Grayndler, with his solar-powered wheelie bin sound systems a fixture around the inner west.
He said AI could be “good for humanity” but is now an “extraction industry mining for profit for the few”.
“I’m completely against [the federal government’s proposal],” he said.

“There’s obviously an AI gold rush at the moment, it’s the wild west and we really need to push back. It’s hard enough being a starving artist these days without having all your work taken and used in these nefarious ways.”
This year Strong curated a show called “overthrow the algorithm”. He has also been a vocal critic of a proposed datacentre at Cooks Cove.
“I’ve seen a backlash [to the government] already,” he said. “It started with the datacentre uprising.”

Labor’s proposals were leaked in September as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met Labor ministers and warned that Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company from training models locally.
For the inner west designer and artist Lu Campbell-Smith, AI has been useful in her practice. But she said having to opt out was “outrageous”.
“It just really pinpoints how Australia’s [a] test market and they’re happy for us to just be a little resource to be exploited,” she said.
“Why would anyone want to make anything and post anything online if … you’re creating free content for an AI machine?”

blocks.caption: Lu Campbell-Smith at her desk in Tortuga Studio’s co-working space called the aerie. Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian

blocks.text: Grayndler has always been an ultra-safe Labor seat. Albanese’s face as a much younger man is plastered on to cans of Albo Pale Ale at Willie the Boatman brewery in St Peters. For the past few elections, he has won on first preferences alone.
But at the next federal election, he will be challenged by 28-year-old Hannah Ferguson, the co-founder of Cheek Media, who will run as an independent.
after newsletter promotion

No sitting member has lost their seat from such a margin at a federal election. Were it not for the longstanding popularity of Albanese, Grayndler would have been a prime target for the Greens and progressive independents.

Now, Ferguson is betting that his popularity is waning. And polling indicates the same. Guardian Australia’s latest Essential poll shows Albanese’s disapproval rating at 56%, the equal highest since he took office.

blocks.caption: A moss-covered computer artwork by Morgan-Harris sits beside the entry to the aerie. Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian

blocks.text: At Tortuga Studios and the aerie, one of the longest-running artist-led spaces in Sydney which operates out of an old brick factory in St Peters, the frustration is palpable.
H Morgan-Harris, an author, curator and director of the space, said there was a risk the Australian creative ecosystem could be “decimated”.

“This whole conversation always comes back to money,” she said, adding: “The artistic ecosystem is the bedrock of human interaction and human connection. And you risk our societal value by threatening it.”

Morgan-Harris’s copywriting industry has already been “heavily impacted” by AI, she said. Asked what her response was to the federal government’s latest proposal, she said it wasn’t “one you can print”.
“I just feel like artists are the first to be thrown under the bus,” she said.

“I think a lot of people were really excited when [Albanese] got into government, but there’s a yawning chasm in terms of the recognition, consideration and protection of the value of this sector. This honestly feels like the end of times to a lot of us.”

blocks.caption: Tortuga Studios has been running for 19 years and provides a hub for artists, designers and craftspeople in Sydney’s inner west. Photograph: Liz Ham/The Guardian

blocks.text: Jason Zoidberg, a co-founder of Monster Mouse Studios in Marrickville, said the AI industry had already “without consequence” stolen the “collective labour” uploaded by artists. He said it was “utterly crazy” that the government was considering giving companies the green light to do so.
“It just feels insane that they’re like, ‘Yeah, please come and we want to invest in you,’ when we’ve seen all these horrible things that they’re doing,” he said.
If there is a flipside, Zoidberg said, he is witnessing a surge in interest in traditional, hands-on art forms.
“There’s a backlash in the inner west against social media and AI,” Zoidberg said. “So our workshops are actually getting more participants. But it is also just a niche, a little inner west bubble.”

articles.title: More than 290 arrested in France as some weekend protests turn violent
articles.summary: Protests continue across France as 320,000 people take to the streets over rising living costs and poor school conditions for a third consecutive weekend, with clashes reported in several cities.

image.caption: The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people had participated in demonstrations across the country, including 70,000 in Paris.Image: Sylvain Thomas/AFP

blocks.text: A number of clashes have been reported between protesters and police in several French cities on Saturday as hundreds of thousands of people again took to the streets nationwide to protest the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.

blocks.caption: France has seen weeks of widespread anger and weekend protests over the rising cost of living and growing inequalityImage: Matthieu Rondel/AFP

blocks.text: 'Radical elements' attempted to enter some city centers
The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people had participated in demonstrations across the country, including 70,000 in Paris.

"The marches proceeded smoothly within the framework of the declared demonstrations," the ministry said, while noting that "radical elements" in several cities, including Bordeaux, Toulouse and Marseille, had attempted to enter city centres "with the aim of carrying out vandalism and looting."
In Marseille, footage showed fires burning in the streets as firefighters responded. Clashes with police were also reported in Rennes and Toulouse.

After a largely peaceful start to the day, police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon in the late afternoon, according to French media reports and live broadcast footage. Tensions in the capital escalated as demonstrators reached the end of their march on the city's southern outskirts.
Footage aired by BFMTV showed fireworks exploding and incendiary devices being thrown at officers in riot gear, with several officers caught in the flames.

blocks.caption: Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were mobilized across the countryImage: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

blocks.text: Police arrest more than 290 people across France
Paris police carried out more than 1,200 checks at railway stations and nearby areas early on Saturday to identify potential troublemakers, the city's police prefecture said.
The checks aimed to prevent demonstrators from bringing fireworks, knives and other prohibited items to the marches.

Police also deployed "all available resources" in the air to monitor security throughout the day, the prefecture said. An official order authorized camera-equipped drones to capture and transmit live images of the situation across the capital.
More than 290 arrests were made on Saturday across France, accorindg to police.

blocks.caption: Authorities also feared that Halloween celebrations could give people an opportunity to conceal their identitiesImage: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

blocks.text: Preparations ahead of the protests
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned earlier Saturday that the demonstrations posed a "very high risk," citing calls for looting and rioting.
Around 70,000 police officers and other security personnel were deployedacross the country to maintain order during the protests.
Authorities also feared that Halloween celebrations could give people an opportunity to conceal their identities while committing offenses.
Amid concerns over attacks on public buildings and looting, officials ordered protest routes in Paris and other cities to be moved away from city centers.

Many shops and businesses responded by boarding up their windows and taking other precautions. Curfews and other restrictions were also imposed in several cities, including measures targeting specific areas and minors.

blocks.caption: A car burns during protests over living costs and education in Paris on Saturday, October 31Image: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Third consecutive weekend of mass action
A similarly large security deployment last weekend largely prevented a repeat of the violence and destruction seen during the October 17 protests.

Young people have been taking to the streets for weeks to protest inadequate staffing and equipment in schools. Since mid-October, other groups have joined the demonstrations, mainly over the rising cost of living.
Trade unions, school and student organizations, and the grassroots Yellow Vest movement, which first rose to prominence in France in 2018, called for Saturday's protests.
France: Why students are taking to the streets

articles.title: Police clash with masked rioters after largely peaceful protests across France
articles.summary:
Demonstrations also taking place in Germany, where officers fire teargas to disperse crowds as evening falls

Clashes have erupted in Paris, Marseille and other cities after tens of thousands…

blocks.text: Clashes have erupted in Paris, Marseille and other cities after tens of thousands of demonstrators, some in Halloween fancy dress, marched across France in a third wave of protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services.

About 320,000 people – down from an estimated 410,000 last weekend – took part in rallies around the country, the interior ministry said, including 70,000 in Paris who marched along boulevards on the south-eastern outskirts, avoiding the city centre.

As evening approached and the largely peaceful demonstrations came to an end, police in several cities fired teargas and stun grenades to disperse crowds joined – as on the previous Saturday – by groups of masked rioters.

blocks.caption: A protester wearing a Marie-Antoinette costume holds a placard reading ‘Give them brioche’ flanked by a protester dressed as a wizard holding a placard reading ‘A potion for the revolution’ during a demonstration in Lyon, France on 31 October 2026. Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: France’s interior minister, Laurent ⁠Nuñez, said earlier this week 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the protests’ sidelines, warning that Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day.

The Paris protesters set off peacefully from the Porte de Bagnolet near the ring road, holding placards with slogans including “No need for teargas to make our future look bleak” and “Disguised as an angry citizen for Halloween”, as a helicopter flew overhead

On and around its destination, the Porte de Charenton, dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police, and at least one incendiary device was thrown at security forces, French media reported.

Police responded with teargas and baton charges. “A hardcore of several hundred rioters” was attacking police with projectiles including a molotov cocktail, the Paris police prefecture said. Officers were “manoeuvring to restore public order”, it added.

In Lyon protesters threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire teargas, and in Toulouse police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators.

The marches brought together school students, who have been calling for better conditions for a month, trade unions and gilets jaune (yellow vests) protesters united in anger at the cost of living, widening inequalities and Emmanuel Macron’s ⁠government.

“The French economy is doing badly no matter what happens, because today we’re being run by a group of incompetents who juggle billions while families are struggling with a few cents,” said one protester on the Paris march, Jérôme Rodrigues. “That’s why we’re here, to keep shouting our demands louder and ‌louder.”

blocks.caption: Protesters wearing Halloween costumes pose in front of the French national flag during a demonstration in Lyon, 31 October 2026. Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A protester in Nantes, Camille Guérin, said: “We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students’ demands, yes to giving citizens a voice.”

Saturday’s rallies came two weeks after widespread street violence and looting rocked numerous French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October that became one of the worst days of civil unrest in the country’s recent history.

Student protesters vowed to stage new high school and university blockades on Tuesday and Thursday. “Then we will join the 5 November demonstration called by workers and trade unions,” said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Étudiante, a student organisation.

blocks.caption: Protesters light smoke flares after a demonstration organised by ‘GenZ regelt!’ (Gen Z has got this!) in Berlin on 31 October 2026.  Photograph: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Protests also took place elsewhere in Europe. In Germany, police fired water cannon to disperse protesters who hurled firework and other projectiles at the end of youth-led protests organised by a group called “Gen Z regelt!” (Gen Z will sort this).

Thousands of police were deployed across the country, with tensions rising as evening fell after mostly peaceful demonstrations for “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life” in dozens of cities.

In the western city of Cologne, police fired water cannon to disperse a crowd after saying protesters had targeted officers with fireworks, and a march was also temporarily halted in Frankfurt after protesters set off fireworks.
In Berlin, protesters hurled bottles and eggs while protesters set barricades ablaze in Hamburg, and police were using pepper spray on demonstrators in some places, the newspaper Bild reported.
Police were also on alert in Barcelona after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings, and in Italy after recent clashes with protesters in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

articles.title: Virginia and DC sue to stop Trump’s arch as government looks to start construction
articles.summary:
Legal challenges to Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting even as its construction is imminent

The legal challenges to

blocks.text: The legal challenges to Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting, with the District of Columbia and Virginia suing in federal court on Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week.

There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250ft (76 meters) on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with the Arlington national cemetery. That would make the arch 100ft taller (30 meters) than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch.

The US district judge Tanya Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against the Trump administration by three Vietnam war veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing on Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously.

In the latest lawsuit, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb of Washington DC and Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that “as soon as defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia. The arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River. During the three-year period of construction, the arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and storm water runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges.”
As the original plaintiffs have, they also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration’s plans to move ahead imminently with construction.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would affect emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, and where a January 2025 midair collision between a US military helicopter and passenger airliner killed 67 people.

The Republican administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a Trump favorite, at Thursday’s meeting of the Capital National Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the two pending lawsuits.

On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an “occupied roof” and two mezzanines.

Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a “fire command center”. The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.

articles.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
articles.summary: Two analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprit.

blocks.text: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.
It said it had replenished the assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.

items: From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean

blocks.text: The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.

The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group called The Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor, as the likely culprits.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange last year.
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

articles.title: More than 50m Americans cast ballots in early voting with three days to go before midterms
articles.summary:
Record number of early votes cast, with Democrats outnumbering Republicans in states which collect that information

There has been a surge of early voting for the US midterm elections, with…

blocks.text: There has been a surge of early voting for the US midterm elections, with millions more Americans going to the polls compared with the last such election amid a series of tight contests that will determine control of Congress.

More than 50.5m early votes have been cast across the US as of Saturday morning, according to an analysis by the University of Florida. This is already nearly 5m more votes than the total number of early votes made in the last midterm elections, in 2022.

Voter enthusiasm for Tuesday’s election appears to be strongest among Democrats, with 10.7 million registered Democrats having voted so far, according to the states that collate such information, compared with 7.8 million registered Republicans.

These party affiliations are not indicative of actual votes cast but polling has shown widespread unhappiness with the presidency of Donald Trump and unusually close races in states usually won comfortably by Republicans.

Republicans are defending a 53-47 Senate majority in a midterm election in which the battleground map has expanded significantly, with Democrats aiming to pull off victories in traditionally conservative-leaning states such as Texas, Alaska and even Kansas that could allow them to take control of the Senate.

In Texas, a state central to Democratic ambitions, more than 7 million people have already voted early, University of Florida data shows. This is already 1.5 million more people than the number who voted early in the state during the 2022 midterms.
In Harris county, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday, an Associated Press analysis found, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022.

The surge comes in a county that has reliably voted Democratic in recent elections, though by varying margins. In 2024, Kamala Harris defeated Trump there by nearly 6% in the presidential contest, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred carried the county by roughly 11% over the Republican incumbent senator Ted Cruz.

This year, the state’s Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, faces Democrat James Talarico in a closely watched Senate race, while the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, is seeking re-election against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the Senate race as Republicans fight to defend a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades. Trump visited Texas earlier this week, his third trip there in a month.

In other close-fought Senate races, early voting has also increased in these midterms, according to the AP. In South Carolina, which Trump won by nearly 18% in the 2024 president election, early voting is up 83% compared with the 2022 midterms.

In Kansas, where another unusually tight Senate battle is under way in a normally reliable Republican state, early voting is up 34%, while in Maine early voting is up 44%. In Michigan, the site of another key Senate race, early voting is up 32%.

The midterms will decide the composition of the US House of Representatives and Senate for the final two years of Trump’s second term, with the rising costs of food, gasoline and other essentials, as well as the Iran war and concern over government corruption, forming the backdrop to the voting.

Trump, weighed down by deep unpopularity among voters, has sought to boost struggling Republican candidates with rallies held across various previously safe states. This effort has included the US president commenting repeatedly on the physical appearance of candidates and dismissing alarm over rising gasoline costs as secondary to the profits of fossil fuel companies.

Trump hinted at the toil of this effort at a rally in Florida on Friday night. “I thought this was it,” he said. “I thought I could relax. Twenty-eight days of this crap in a row is a lot. It’s a lot.”

articles.title: PDRF to close gaps in Philippines water security
articles.summary: The Philippines has plenty of water, yet many families, cities and businesses still face shortages, floods and unreliable supply.

blocks.text: November 1, 2026 | 12:00am
The NWRB, PDRF and the city governments of Antipolo and Baguio hold a panel discussion on a project linking private sector expertise with national and local government water priorities.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has plenty of water, yet many families, cities and businesses still face shortages, floods and unreliable supply.

To close that gap, the Philippine Disaster Resilience Foundation recently brought together national agencies, local governments, water utilities and its member-companies for Cluster Connect: Public-Private Collaboration for Water Resilience in Makati City.

The event also marked the official launch of the Building Resilience through Inclusive Development and Gender Equality (BRIDGE) project, a four-year initiative implemented by PDRF and funded by the government of Canada to strengthen water management and climate resilience in Antipolo City and Baguio City.
Water problems in the Philippines come from many directions at once: changing weather patterns, damaged watersheds, fast-growing cities, rising demand and gaps in infrastructure.

Many agencies, LGUs and private groups are working to address these challenges, but these efforts are not always aligned or coordinated. Cluster Connect, an annual gathering of PDRF’s cluster members to strengthen private sector coordination and align with the country’s resilience agenda, aims to bring these efforts together into a coordinated approach where the government sets direction, LGUs lead on the ground and business brings resources and expertise.

“Canada is proud to support the Philippines’ efforts to strengthen water security, recognizing that access to safe, reliable and sustainable water resources is essential for healthy communities, economic growth and climate resilience. Canada’s experience has shown that sustainable water solutions are built through strong partnerships across government, the private sector and communities, bringing together policy leadership, innovation, technology and investment,” said Canadian Ambassador David Hartman.

articles.title: House to comply with SC order on impeachment vote threshold
articles.summary: The House of Representatives will comply with the order of the Supreme Court to comment on a petition challenging the validity of the Senate impeachment court’s ruling to lower the voting…

blocks.text: November 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Facade of the House of Representatives at the Batasan Complex in Quezon City.
The STAR / Michael Varcas, File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The House of Representatives will comply with the order of the Supreme Court to comment on a petition challenging the validity of the Senate impeachment court’s ruling to lower the voting threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.
House prosecution panel spokesman Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said they will comply with the order as the panel remained focused on presenting evidence against Duterte.
He said the high court’s request is only a routine court procedure but did not indicate a timeline on when the panel will submit its response.
“This is just the usual procedure that we expect the court to issue,” he said.

The SC also ordered the Senate to file a comment on the petition filed by Sens. Robin Padilla and Bong Go, staunch allies of Duterte, along with officials of the opposition party Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan, which sought the issuance of a temporary restraining order and/or a status quo ante order against the Sept. 23 decision of the impeachment court to lower the vote threshold.
The Senate voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict on the number of senators who are capable of “legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings.”

As a result, the vote threshold for the conviction of Duterte may move from 16 to 14 votes, considering that Sens. Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder charges, Sen. Loren Legarda has been on an extended medical leave abroad and Sen. Ronald dela Rosa has been in hiding since May.
“We respect the Supreme Court and we will comply with whatever the issuances from the Supreme Court would cover in relation to the petition filed by two sitting senator-judges,” Adiong said.
Asked whether the prosecution would reaffirm the Senate ruling, Adiong said determining the voting requirement was not the role of the prosecution.
“Our position is to present the evidence necessary to prove our case,” he said.

He said it was the impeachment court that determined how to apply the voting requirement and the prosecution’s responsibility was to support the remaining Article II (unexplained wealth) allegations with the records and testimony presented to the panel.
Adiong also pointed out that neither party had requested the ruling, placing responsibility for the procedural decision with the Senate sitting as an impeachment court.
“Neither the prosecution nor the defense asked for it,” he said.

articles.title: More Canadian provinces are ditching the time change. But did they pick the wrong option?

image.caption: People face the Clock Tower in Montreal on Wednesday. As parts of Canada stop changing their clocks twice a year, sleep scientists say the time they've chosen to keep could have consequences for sleep and health. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada
Researchers are raising concerns as parts of Canada move to permanent daylight time, warning that later winter sunrises could have consequences for sleep and health.
Sleep scientists say ending the switch is good, but permanent daylight is the wrong choice

Millions of Canadians will turn their clocks back one hour this weekend, while millions of others will not. This divide is putting Canadians under different time systems — with potentially different consequences for their health.

Most of British Columbia, as well as Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories are no longer changing their clocks twice a year, joining Yukon and Saskatchewan. Most of Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces will still turn their clocks back on Nov. 1 for the end of daylight saving time.

For Quebec, this could be the last time. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced Wednesday that his government is moving to end the twice-yearly clock change, but it has not yet decided which time the province will keep. He said that decision will be made after consulting experts.

Research suggests permanent standard time — the time we return to in the fall — is more closely aligned with the body's internal clock than permanent daylight time, which several provinces have chosen.
Here's what winter time would look like across Canada under proposed time-zone changes

Joseph De Koninck, an emeritus professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa, has studied sleep for decades. He said the springtime change is the most problematic because people lose an hour of sleep when they set their clocks forward, creating a mismatch between the body's internal biological clock and solar time.

De Koninck explained that our biological clock uses light to synchronize itself. As daylight changes with the seasons, our circadian rhythms adjust gradually. Making a one-hour adjustment all at once, however, is much more difficult.
"We are able to adapt, but it's not optimal for our health."
The Edmonton skyline at dawn. As one of Canada's northernmost major cities, Edmonton will see winter sunrises as late as 10 a.m. under Alberta's new permanent daylight time. (John Robertson/CBC)
Why morning light matters
Michael Antle, head of the University of Calgary's psychology department and a professor who studies circadian rhythms, said permanent standard time would have been better for Alberta.
Because of the province's northern latitude and position within its time zone, it already has late winter sunrises, Antle said. Permanent daylight time will push them forward another hour.
"It's not the choice I would have made," he said of the province's decision.

items: Cross Country Checkup is asking: What questions do you have about getting a good night's sleep? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

blocks.text: Antle said daylight time essentially means society has agreed to get up and go to work or school an hour earlier.
Most people's circadian clocks run slightly slow, making them somewhat "night owlish," he said. Morning light helps speed up that clock.
Michael Antle, a University of Calgary psychology professor, says permanent standard time is healthier because it better aligns with people's body clocks. (Submitted by Michael Antle)
When morning light arrives later, there can be a mismatch between what the body wants to do and what work or school requires.
Antle described this effect as "social jetlag."

Antle pointed to population studies that found people exposed to later sunsets slept less and had higher rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. He also cited Russian research that found winter depression among young people increased while Russia observed permanent daylight time.
Why some scientists don't support B.C.'s switch to permanent daylight time
Why researchers say permanent daylight time is a bad idea
Both researchers distinguish between the disruption caused by changing the clocks and the effects of living on daylight time year-round.

Antle said the spring change creates a sudden shift that can leave people feeling as though they're living on the wrong time for several weeks. Permanent daylight time would extend that mismatch through the darkest months of the year.
He would prefer permanent standard time. Continuing to spring forward and fall back would be a compromise, he said, preserving later summer evenings without the longer-term winter mismatch.

items: For thousands of workers, lifelong time-zone math will go out the window when B.C. stops changing clocks
Time zones in Canada are getting complicated. These maps lay them out

blocks.text: Night owls who work regular daytime jobs may struggle the most because they already find it difficult to wake up early, Antle said.

Those darker mornings are also having a real-world impact. Ski hills in Alberta's Bow Valley, for example, are delaying their opening times this winter to give staff more daylight to prepare the slopes before skiers arrive.
But most schools and workplaces have less flexibility to change their hours based on when the sun is up.
Changing clocks twice a year a question of public health: prof
Canada becomes a natural experiment
Canada's emerging patchwork could give researchers an opportunity to study neighbouring populations living under different time systems.
Antle said he would have preferred a year's notice to collect baseline data before Alberta made the change.
He said researchers should examine mental health, vehicle and pedestrian collisions, school performance and attendance, and workplace attendance and tardiness.
De Koninck noted that researchers now have tools to document sleep habits over time and compare how people adapt in different provinces.

But he expects Western Canadians may make their feelings known before researchers have years of data to analyze. People may not fully understand what permanent daylight time means, he said, until they've experienced a winter with much later sunrises.
"Those who've tried it haven't liked it," he said.
For De Koninck, the larger concern is what prolonged sleep disruption can mean for people's health.
"If you feel sleep deprived, then you have a host of issues, psychological and physical," he said.
"You can't play with your sleep."

articles.title: Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push
articles.summary:
But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote

In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support…

blocks.text: In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusing Republicans of protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
The ads appear intended to evoke an emotional response by accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.

An analysis from CNN found that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Another from the Washington Post found that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.

In Colorado, ads targeting Republican Jeff Crank note that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files. In one, the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”.
Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa, was accused of voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.
“This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinson said in a campaign ad responding to attacks over the Epstein files.

An ad targeting Mike Collins, the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”.
Florida Republican Jimmy Patronis faced an attack from his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”.

A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement to the Washington Post, because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”.

Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, the New York Times reported. Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.

Last year, Democrats and a select few House Republicans tried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.

Donald Trump, who knew Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files, reversing his campaign promise to increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.

Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.
Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.
after newsletter promotion

“Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.

Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, but told a local radio station that while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”.

Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.”
Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusing Democrats of taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.

During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman has said he only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.
“You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,” Collins said.

In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside group released an ad accusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”.
Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014. Haaland has said she was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.

articles.title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
articles.summary: Government data shows that more than 10,000 people have contracted the rare virus.

blocks.text: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.
Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.
The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.

In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.
Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations, and the second largest in history.
The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.
Testing and treatment is under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.
The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is currently no treatment or vaccine for this strain.
Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.

Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.

Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.
No cases have been reported in Uganda since August, but travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.
In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths. One woman was confirmed to have the disease in Nigeria, but flown to Switzerland for further treatment.
The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

articles.title: Ethiopian PM puts ministers through military training
articles.summary: The prime minister has previously emphasised military preparedness as central to his government's ambitions.

blocks.text: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.
Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.
The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.
Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.
It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.

In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.
He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.

"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.
Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.
The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.
It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.
Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

blocks.text: Toronto·
Toronto police will be updating the public at 10 a.m. Saturday on the investigation into the home invasion that took place in the Bridle Path neighbourhood earlier this week.
Police requested public's help in identifying three suspects on Friday
Toronto police give update on home invasion probe
Toronto police will be updating the public Saturday morning on the investigation into the home invasion that took place in the Bridle Path neighbourhood earlier this week.
Officers responded to reports of a "violent home invasion" at a residence near Hyde Park Circle and Post Road Thursday morning, Toronto police said Thursday.

Police said three suspects, armed with handguns and a hammer, forced their way into the home, made demands for valuables and attacked four adults in the home — a 75-year-old father, 64-year-old mother and their 26 and 28-year-old daughters.
The news conference on Saturday will take place at 10 a.m. with updates from Insp. Kristy Smith of the Toronto police's Hold Up Squad.

David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, said three members of his family are recovering in hospital after they were shot during the home invasion. All four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer, he said in an emailed statement issued Friday.
David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, a real estate group, said his family is 'traumatized' after they suffered a violent and 'horrific' home invasion in their Bridle Path home Thursday. (macsuites.ca)
"No family should ever have to experience this," he said, adding the family is traumatized and recovering after the attack on Thursday.
On Friday, police requested the public's help to identify and locate the three suspects, who fled the area in a dark coloured SUV.
The suspects are described as men in their 20s wearing dark clothing and face masks.
All three men are considered to be armed and dangerous, police said.
