articles.title: Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Belarus on their way to Ukraine
articles.summary: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine arrived in Belarus on Saturday on their way back to Ukraine, part of a major rescue operation carried out under the most significant truce since…

image.caption: Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, left, and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, centre, speak with journalists on Friday before departing for Oleshky to evacuate local residents to a safe area during a local ceasefire. (Office of the Ombudsman of Ukraine/The

blocks.text: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine arrived in Belarus on Saturday on their way back to Ukraine, part of a major rescue operation carried out under the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.

The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, which the White House says was brokered with help from U.S. first lady Melania Trump, began at 3 a.m. local time on Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
It was a rare joint Russia-Ukraine humanitarian effort — a brief respite in the grim war.

Civilians from Oleshky, on the Dnipro River, began the long journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday. The estimated 2,000 remaining residents were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said those who chose to travel from Oleshky to Ukrainian-held territory were taken to the Russian city of Anapa and flown to the Belarusian city of Homel. They were accompanied by Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, it said.
"We will be home soon!" said a video post from Lubinets at Homel airport.
Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire area expands in eastern Ukraine
Four planes with the evacuees landed in Belarus and the passengers would be on Ukrainian territory "within hours," said Ukrainian lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia.
Daughters wait to see their fathers again
Relatives waited on Saturday at the border between Ukraine and Belarus, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them.
Volunteers from organizations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.

items: Aid operation, evacuations underway in Ukraine's stricken city of Oleshky

blocks.text: Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father more than two years ago, was among those waiting. Paliy, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory at the time, while he stayed behind.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
U.S.-brokered ceasefire begins in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbours but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no [other] way, and he walked us to the road and that was it," Pavlyn said of the last time she saw her father.

items: Russia, Ukraine team up on relief effort in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Melania Trump, Pope Leo broker humanitarian ceasefire for ravaged Ukraine city Oleshky

blocks.text: She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

Russia's ombudsperson and lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia. Russian media outlets on Saturday showed civilians arriving at a temporary accommodation site in Simferopol on the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
A humanitarian convoy carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, Ukraine, drives along a road in Armyansk in Crimea on Friday. (Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters)

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
U.S. approves Patriot missile sales for Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday welcomed U.S. approval of Ukraine’s purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors but urged partners to supply the weapons from existing stocks to protect the country this winter, warning the newly authorized U.S. sale could take years to deliver.

"Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
24 hours in Kyiv: Living through Russian drone strikes

The Trump administration said Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion US sale of Patriot air defence interceptors, after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of the vital munition needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles.
The U.S. State Department said 500 Patriot missiles would be purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.
A Ukrainian drone attack kills 2 in Russia

Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.

items: Russia, Ukraine begin ceasefire in city of Oleshky as deadly strikes continue elsewhere
Melania Trump, Pope Leo broker humanitarian ceasefire for ravaged Ukraine city Oleshky

blocks.text: Russia's Ministry of Defence said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.
B.C. animal rescuer killed by drone on Ukraine's front lines
Zelenskyy urged partners to impose further sanctions on Russia and provide new support packages to Ukraine.
"The world sees Russia targeting civilian infrastructure every day. Everyone who does not want to see this Russian escalation spread further into Europe must help Ukraine," he said in an online post.

articles.title: France braces for 3rd weekend of discord as youth-led protests spread across Europe
articles.summary: France prepared Saturday for a third consecutive weekend of protests over living costs and education, deploying 70,000 police and gendarmes and rerouting the Paris march to the capital's edge as…

image.caption: A man stands in front of a barricaded shop of the soccer team Paris Saint-Germain before protests over living costs and education get underway in Paris on Saturday. (Emma Da Silva/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

France prepared Saturday for a third consecutive weekend of protests over living costs and education, deploying 70,000 police and gendarmes and rerouting the Paris march to the capital's edge as youth-led demonstrations spread across Europe.
High school students began demonstrating against school conditions last month
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween.

Paris police banned union and "yellow vest" marches through the city centre, ordering demonstrations to follow a single route along the capital's outer boulevards, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton. Unions and student groups challenged the restrictions in court but lost in a last-minute legal battle.
Students in France clash with riot police amid weekslong education protests
President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that marches would stay out of city centres to protect shops.
Police also barred entry to Place de la République and Les Halles, both hit by rioting and looting on Oct. 17, Saturday night into Sunday morning.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Élysées. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protesters scuffle with riot police during a demonstration against rising living costs, in Paris on Oct. 17. (Emma Da Silva/The Associated Press)
The movement began with high school students protesting school conditions and broadened into anger over living costs.

Authorities counted about 550,000 protesters nationwide on Oct. 17, when rioters looted hundreds of shops, and 410,000 last Saturday, when rallies were largely peaceful, but police made more than 1,300 arrests.

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — urged protests in some 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life" and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said more than 140,000 people had signed up online.

items: What's behind the youth protests in France?
Tens of thousands march in France as protests continue over schools and living costs

blocks.text: Berlin police expected about 10,000 people at the Brandenburg Gate. Some shops on the Kurfürstendamm boulevard boarded up their windows, although authorities said they were unaware of specific threats of violence. Protests were expected to begin in the early afternoon.

In Barcelona, Catalan police planned to activate their highest-level alert after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings. Rioting in the Spanish city last Saturday led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.
Italian police were on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna, and calls to protest circulated on TikTok in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.

articles.title: Parks Canada set to slash warden detachments, officers across national parks
articles.summary: Detachments will be closing in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Northwest Territories. The number of wardens impacted by the decision is unknown, but CBC News…

image.caption: These changes come amidst $145 million in cuts to Parks Canada over the next three years. (Parks Canada)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Detachments will be closing in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Northwest Territories. The number of wardens impacted by the decision is unknown, but CBC News has learned at least a dozen positions will be cut.
Federal agency spokesperson says it 'will continue to provide services across all locations'
Parks Canada is closing at least 13 warden detachments and prioritizing a regional service for law enforcement, according to multiple sources.
Detachments will be closing in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Northwest Territories.

The number of wardens impacted by the decision is unknown, but CBC News has learned at least a dozen positions will be cut. Some detachments, such as Banff and Jasper, will each lose one warden, multiple sources told CBC News.
"We’re deeply concerned what that looks like. These aren’t just administrative changes," said Krysty Thomas, regional executive vice-president for Public Service Alliance of Canada’s Prairies region.

"We’re talking about highly trained officers who play an important role in protecting our national parks, enforcing environmental laws and providing critical support to other employees working in the field."
These changes come amidst $145 million in cuts to Parks Canada over the next three years.

Parks Canada acting CEO and vice-president of transformation Andrew Campbell wrote in an Oct. 20 email to staff that 2,917 letters went out to employees to let them know they could move to new jobs or be let go. Thomas said the union has been told Parks Canada plans to cut 517 full-time jobs.

items: Parks Canada plan to cut 500 jobs draws criticism from union

blocks.text: Among the detachments closing will be Kluane National Park in Yukon, Kejimkujik National Park in Nova Scotia, Elk Island National Park in Alberta and Point Pelee National Park in Ontario. Others are Gulf Islands National Park Reserve in British Columbia, Fundy National Park in New Brunswick and Nahanni National Park Reserve in Northwest Territories.
A new regional system will have 85 total wardens spread over western, central, eastern and northern Canada, and the Rockies.
Thomas said PSAC wants to hear how Parks Canada will “maintain these important services with fewer people in fewer locations.”

Meaghan Bradley, a spokesperson in Parks Canada’s national communications office, told CBC News the federal agency is “modernizing its law enforcement model by redistributing capacity to focus on areas of highest priority and risk.”

Bradley didn’t acknowledge the number of wardens being let go, but said “some detachments are being consolidated into higher-need areas” and "adopting a more intelligence-driven approach to enforcement," including adding three regional intelligence co-ordinator positions.

CBC News reached out via email to the leadership team in charge of the decision-making for the cuts. Campbell, executive director of transformation Hugues Michaud, transformation communications Stéphane Rondeau and senior strategic adviser Laurie Wein didn't get back to CBC News.
Multiple other requests for interviews were also declined.
Some of the 34 national park wardens who received the Peace Officer Exemplary Service Medal in Banff on Oct. 21, 2025. (Parks Canada)
'You just get burned out'
When a detachment in a national park is closed, it means there's no on-the-ground law enforcement. The new system will rely on bringing in regional wardens to enforce federal law.

Mike Henderson was a warden in the Canadian Rockies for more than 30 years until retiring in 2022. He said a regional plan could contribute to staff burnout, especially if they’re thinly stretched to cover vast territories.

If a warden in the Lake Louise, Yoho, Kootenay field unit were to get a call on the Icefields Parkway, for instance, it could take more than half a shift to respond and get to another call, Henderson said.

“If you’re relying on the bigger national parks to fill the holes required in smaller national parks, you’re still pulling somebody from a bigger place,” he said. “You still don’t have enough staff. It’s not really a Band-Aid solution. It’s a way to muddle your way through.”

items: Parks Canada ends search and rescue dog program

blocks.text: He noted the majority of warden work is a one-person job in remote areas — a mixture of front country and back country work.
“You go to these calls and you know you’re by yourself. … You just get burned out,” he said.
“That’s the weird thing with wardening: it’s pretty smooth sailing until it’s not.”
Thomas said “one of the most troubling things they’re hearing” is staff may be without backup in remote locations.
“Worker safety cannot be an afterthought in the workforce reduction exercise,” she said.
The former warden cabin near the Iceline Trail in Yoho National Park on Oct. 4, 2026. (Greg Colgan/CBC)
'Parks Canada has a responsibility to protect these places for future generations'
Parks Canada’s executive director of conservation Tamaini Snaith presented the changes in an Oct. 22 virtual meeting with wardens across the country, according to multiple sources.
Multiple sources told CBC News that people in some of the positions being cut will be offered roles in the new regional enforcement areas.

items: Parks Canada not laying charges after Banff National Park superintendent admits to violating federal law

blocks.text: Parks Canada did an evaluation of the law enforcement program in 2023. The report states it has an annual budget of about $10 million, with roughly 80 per cent allocated to salaries.

It notes there were about 100 wardens in 2022. Through surveys and interviews, it found “there is also agreement that available resources have not kept pace with the increasing needs of the program” since new national parks have been created and laws have increased responsibilities.

Parks Canada administers more than 450,000 square kilometres of land and water in 37 national parks, 11 national park reserves, five national marine conservation areas, one national urban park and 171 national historic sites.
Bradley said some positions will be relocated, and the warden service “will continue to provide services across all locations.”
Thomas said the union has been asking Parks Canada about impacts to response times, increased travel distances and what happens when a warden needs immediate backup.

“These are occupational health and safety concerns and not just financial savings. ... Parks Canada has a responsibility to protect these places for future generations," she said. "That responsibility doesn’t disappear because budgets are being reduced.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Greg Colgan is a journalist for CBC in the Bow Valley. He was previously the editor of the Rocky Mountain Outlook in Banff and Canmore. He has also worked for media outlets in Ontario and has experience covering topics such as sports, politics, housing and development, courts and arts and entertainment. He joined CBC in 2025. He can be reached at greg.colgan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Undas 2026: Flooding hits Iloilo cemetery; flower prices surge in Cotabato
articles.summary: A day before All Saints" Day, Filipinos have begun visiting cemeteries across the country to pay their respects to departed loved ones, with some areas reporting flooding and higher flower prices…

blocks.text: Published October 31, 2026 7:44pm

A day before All Saints’ Day, Filipinos have begun visiting cemeteries across the country to pay their respects to departed loved ones, with some areas reporting flooding and higher flower prices ahead of the Undas observance.

According to a social media report by Zen Quilantang-Sasa of GMA Regional TV Ratsada Balita, the Tanza Public Cemetery in Iloilo City was partially flooded on Saturday following heavy morning rainfall.
To help visitors navigate the flooded pathways, several men were seen placing concrete debris and rocks to create makeshift elevated walkways.

PANOORIN: Nagtulungan ang ilang kalalakihan upang malagyan ng madadaanan ng mga bumibisita ang Tanza Public Cemetery sa Iloilo City matapos bahagyang bumaha sa sementeryo dahil sa pagbuhos ng ulan kaninang umaga, Oct. 31. Ayon sa mga bumisita sa kanilang mga yumaong mahal sa buhay, taon-taon nila itong nararanasan tuwing Undas. Umaasa silang kaagad itong mabigyan ng atensyon ng Iloilo City LGU. | via Zen Quilantang-Sasa/GMA Regional TV Ratsada Balita Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JOAN0 para sa pinakabagong balita. Other Stories — GMA News (@gmanews) October 31, 2026
Some visitors appealed to the Iloilo City local government for an immediate solution, saying the flooding has been a recurring problem during Undas whenever it rains.
Flower prices rise in Cotabato City
In Cotabato City, prices of flowers sold at PC Hill in Cotabato City had doubled, Efren Mamac of GMA Regional TV One Mindanao reported.

PANOORIN: Presyo ng bulaklak sa PC Hill, Cotabato City, dumoble ngayong bisperas ng Undas. Ayon sa mga florist, nagkulang daw ang suplay ng mga bulaklak dahil sa mataas na demand ngayong #Undas2026. | via Efren Mamac/GMA Regional TV One Mindanao Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JOAN0 para sa iba pang updates.— GMA News (@gmanews) October 31, 2026
Florists attributed the increase to high demand and limited supply.
“Medyo tumaas at dumoble ang presyo ng mga bulaklak natin ngayon, Sir,” said florist Jay Agan.
(Prices of our flowers have increased, nearly doubling today, Sir.)
Agan added that their flower stocks had already sold out on Friday, October 30.
According to Mamac's report, a pot of chrysanthemums that normally sells for around P150 now costs about P300.
Prices are expected to triple on All Saints’ Day, November 1.
Cemeteries in other provinces
Visitors also flocked to the Baguio City Public Cemetery, where the police recorded more than 700 arrivals as of 10 a.m. on Saturday.
In a report by Jasmin Gabriel-Galban of GMA Regional TV One North Central Luzon, the number of visitors was expected to exceed 5,000 by the end of October 31.

PANOORIN: Aabot na sa mahigit 700 katao ang bumisita sa Baguio City Public Cemetery as of 10 AM ngayong umaga, Oct. 31, 2026, ayon sa Baguio City Police Office. Gardening tools at maging mga alagang aso at pusa, hindi pinayagang makapasok sa loob ng sementeryo. | via Jasmin Gabriel-Galban/GMA Regional TV One North Central Luzon Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JOAN0 para sa pinakabagong balita.— GMA News (@gmanews) October 31, 2026

Police officers were stationed at the cemetery entrance to inspect visitors’ bags. Among the items confiscated were cleaning materials, including hard brooms, as the period for cleaning gravesites had already ended.
As of 10 a.m., no traffic buildup was reported on nearby roads, while the situation inside and outside the cemetery remained orderly.
Taxi and jeepney stands were also set up outside the cemetery to accommodate commuters heading home after visiting their departed loved ones.

Residents of El Salvador City, Misamis Oriental, have begun visiting the graves of their departed loved ones at the Our Lady of the Snow Cemetery ahead of All Saints’ Day, according to GMA Regional TV One Mindanao's Cyril Chaves.
However, several graves remain uncleaned, while some tombs are still damaged, as relatively few visitors have arrived to prepare the gravesites.
—VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Evacuated Ukrainians from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Belarus
articles.summary: Residents were taken out from the devastated city on Friday during a local ceasefire.

blocks.text: Residents evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have arrived in Belarus and are expected back in Ukraine later on Saturday, authorities have said.
They were taken out on Friday during a local ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Planes carrying Oleshky residents landed in the city of Gomel on Saturday morning, according to Belarusian state media and a senior Ukrainian official.

"The last, fourth plane landed in Gomel (Belarus). In a few hours, all Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky, together with the Ukrainian delegation, will be on Ukrainian territory," said David Arakhamia, a key Ukrainian official.
The state-owned Belarusian news agency Belta reported a bus convoy of Oleshky residents had left Gomel airport and was heading towards the Ukrainian border.
A humanitarian ceasefire took force across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday, providing the first few days of peace in the area in four years, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The ceasefire allowed the road out of Oleshky to be demined and will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.
Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and a lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".

articles.title: 'No one is safe' as Ebola outbreak surges to more than 10,000 cases, Africa's top doctor warns Canada
articles.summary: Africa's top doctor, who has called Canada home since 2013, tells CBC News there could be "massive" cross-border spread of Ebola in the months ahead as he calls for more international support.

image.caption: Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, at an emergency meeting of African ministers in late October amid a devastating outbreak of Ebola that's gripped central Africa for most of 2026. (Dr. Jean Kaseya/Africa CDC/X)

blocks.text: Health·Exclusive
Africa's top doctor, who has called Canada home since 2013, tells CBC News there could be "massive" cross-border spread of Ebola in the months ahead as he calls for more international support.
African health official tells CBC News there may be 'massive' cross-border spread, calls on Canada for support

As the world's fastest-growing outbreak of Ebola hit more than 10,000 confirmed cases this week, Africa's top doctor warned there could be "massive" spread into additional countries — and even other continents — unless countries such as Canada offer more support.

"No one is safe today," said Dr. Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), in an interview with CBC News from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Friday.
"We are calling on all African countries to increase the level of preparedness. But we're also calling our Western countries, especially Canada, because Canada is where my heart is."

Kaseya is from Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and has led Africa CDC for the past three years. But he has called Canada home since 2013. He told CBC News he has been living apart from his family — his three children attend university in Toronto, and his wife remains in Laval, Que. — as he works to end an unprecedented crisis that began in his home country.
He singled out Canada as an ally to African health officials, though he said more can still be done.

"This is my message to Canadians: No fear, no panic, but take it seriously, and even talk to your parliamentarians, talk to other people you know, if they can provide more support for this outbreak," he told CBC News.
"I really want to be back home to celebrate with my family, but we need to stop this outbreak before doing that."
Death toll surpasses 5,000

Kaseya's comments follow a grim new milestone in this year's Ebola outbreak. Confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo have surpassed 10,000, while the latest report from the country's public health institute shows the death toll has surpassed 5,000.
The outbreak was first declared in mid-May, but scientists suspect the Bundibugyo strain of the virus had been spreading undetected for months in some of Congo's most remote regions.

items: Ebola cases top 10,000 in Democratic Republic of Congo, as countries race to stop spread
Nigeria Ebola patient flown to Switzerland, Congo health worker killed as 4 countries deal with outbreak

blocks.text: Ongoing conflict, public distrust and the lack of an approved treatment or vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain have further complicated efforts to contain the outbreak.

It is now the country's largest-ever outbreak and the fastest-growing and second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded — behind only the West Africa Ebola crisis, which infected more than 28,000 people, mainly across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, from 2014 to 2016.
"If this outbreak [continues] like that, with the same magnitude, in one year we'll have more than what West Africa had in two years and a half," Kaseya said.
"But it won't be just a few countries. It will be more countries. It can also affect some other continents."
A much smaller number of infections have already appeared in neighbouring countries, including Uganda, Kenya, and most recently in Nigeria, which reported its first Ebola infection in a decade.
That patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, was flown to Switzerland for treatment on Monday, the latest in a series of patients evacuated to European countries since the outbreak began.

items: Fears of a pan-African Ebola crisis growing as fourth country reports first case
1 in 4 Ebola deaths are children in Democratic Republic of Congo's worst outbreak

blocks.text: Kaseya said imported infections could continue as teams on the ground struggle to slow community transmission in new areas of Congo.
The risk to Canada remains low, he added, though he implored Canadian officials to "move from low to zero by supporting [Africa] to stop the outbreak where it is currently."
Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history
Canada offered $8M to Ebola fight

Canada committed $8 million to the Ebola response in May, including $2 million for Africa CDC to accelerate surveillance and strengthen biosecurity measures. In late July, Health Canada also authorized Moderna to launch a clinical trial of its vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo virus.

The federal government also introduced temporary border measures aimed at reducing the risk of Ebola entering and spreading in Canada, including outbreak alerts issued for Kenya and Nigeria in October.

"The Government of Canada will continue to monitor the situation closely and may adjust these measures, as appropriate, based on evolving evidence and the epidemiological situation both in Canada and internationally," the Public Health Agency of Canada told CBC News in a statement this week.

items: Suspected Ebola case at Montreal hospital turns out to be a false alarm
Canada extends Ebola travel restrictions for another 30 days

blocks.text: Alongside those official efforts, Canadian research teams are also working behind the scenes to study this once-rare form of Ebola.

University of Winnipeg microbiologist Jason Kindrachuk said Canadian and Congolese scientists have sequenced more than 1,000 genomes to date, offering insights into how the virus is behaving and whether existing vaccines may offer cross-protection for the Bundibugyo strain.
But he stressed there are "finite resources" for that collaborative, cross-border work.
Congolese students in Montreal separated from loved ones due to Canada travel restrictions
Canadian scientists 'scramble' for research funding

"We're trying to scramble with funds from whatever sources we have to be able to keep things like genome sequencing alive, to keep testing alive … so I think at some point we need to see bigger investment, and certainly sustained investment, from the high-income areas of the world," Kindrachuk said.
"I think there's a real need for Canada and other countries to step up."

Kaseya praised Canada's efforts to date, including the close collaboration between African and Canadian health officials, but agreed that the threat of Ebola could persist for months without broader support to end the crisis.

"We'll continue to work hard to keep Canada safe — we'll do our best to keep all other countries in the world safe — but … if we do not provide support, we cannot guarantee that all of us will be safe," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Pelley is a senior health and medical reporter for CBC News. She's a two-time RNAO Media Award winner for in-depth health reporting in 2020 and 2022, a silver medallist for best editorial newsletter at the 2024 Digital Publishing Awards, and a 2024 Covering Climate Now award winner in the health category. Contact her at: lauren.pelley@cbc.ca.

articles.title: How to tell whether your lithium batteries are a fire risk — and what to do if they are
articles.summary: We've heard a lot about how dangerous lithium battery fires are, but most of us also keep and charge smartphones, e-bikes and other lithium battery devices at home. Do we actually need to worry? Are…

image.caption: Experts warn consumers to watch out for the warning signs of a damaged battery that could start a fire in devices such as cellphones or power banks. (Daniel Krason/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: We've heard a lot about how dangerous hot, fast-moving lithium battery fires are and their rising number — more than 1,500 in communities across Canada last year.
But most of us also keep and charge smartphones, power banks, e-bikes, vacuum cleaners, drills and lots of other lithium battery devices at home without any issues.
So are all the fire warnings overblown? Are some kinds safer than others? Can batteries really go from safe to risky? What are the warning signs? And what should you be doing about this?
How safe are lithium batteries really?
Experts generally agree that overall, lithium batteries are very safe.

Vinny Gupta, assistant professor of fire safety engineering at the University of Waterloo, notes that more than 10 billion battery cells are now manufactured every year. "And we typically only hear about safety issues in just a few of them."

The problem is when the systems fail and they do catch fire, it's "quite dramatic," acknowledged Gupta, who does research that involves intentionally making them fail and catch fire to study their fire risk.
Safety measures typically built into consumer lithium batteries include temperature sensors, pressure relief valves to vent potentially flammable gases and systems to prevent overcharging.
So do you really need to take measures like watching them as they charge and unplugging them as soon as they're done charging, as firefighters advise?
Regina fire chief gives reminder to check charging devices
It's true that the battery should automatically stop charging.
But experts note that a battery that has been safe all along can become a fire risk at some point.
How can a lithium battery that was safe become a fire risk?

David Giles, CEO of TempAlert, a Halifax company that sells heat-sensing battery-monitoring stickers, said even if people are using batteries as intended, they can become damaged and therefore hazardous.
That could be due to a defect. Or it could be due to an event, such as an e-bike or e-scooter collision.
He says that when you drop your phone, you may notice if you crack the screen. "But you also may have done other internal damage that might not show up right away" — including damaging the battery.
TempAlert makes heat-sensitive stickers that change from black to yellow at 60 C, indicating a problem with your battery. (TempAlert)
Heat, such as from charging your battery in the sun, can also cause damage.

Gupta said one of the most common ways to cause a battery to fail is by overcharging it. Typically, batteries are designed to prevent that, but some are more poorly designed than others, and the risk increases if they're tampered with or paired with the wrong charger.

Giles says that's easy to do, since most have connectors that fit into many devices. But he warns they may be designed for different voltages. The wrong charger "could be ramming, you know, 80, 90 volts into a battery only designed for 40. That's when you start having a major problem."
Repeatedly charging and recharging a battery over time can also eventually cause it to wear out and fail.
When that happens, does the battery catch on fire right away?
Here's the good news — usually no.

"Batteries don't just go into thermal runaway instantly," Giles said. Thermal runaway is a term for when a battery starts to rapidly self-heat, generating more heat and creating a feedback loop that can lead to a fire. "It progressively gets worse and worse."
Lithium batteries are found in many devices, including e-bikes, and most are safe. (Grant Linton/CBC)

When a battery first starts failing, it may feel hot to touch while charging — Gupta says that's "the earliest indication" that something is wrong. At that point, it will usually cool when you unplug it.
Giles said that may happen repeatedly before it stays hot even after being unplugged.
So how much time do you really have before you have a dangerous fire?
"To be honest, we don't really know," Gupta said, as it depends on what is going on inside the battery and the self-heating process is exponential once underway.
Giles said it could take days or weeks of charging and use, or it could take just 20 minutes.
What to do when a lithium battery is on fire
Are some kinds of lithium batteries less dangerous from a fire safety perspective?
The short answer is no.
The two most popular lithium battery chemistries are NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) and LFP (lithium iron phosphate), which have different materials in their cathodes.
Several readers wrote in to suggest that LFP is less combustible and prone to overheating.
But in Gupta's opinion, "It's hard to really say if one chemistry is safer than [the] other … there are trade-offs."

It's true that LFP is less energy dense and goes into thermal runaway at a higher temperature (about 235 C, compared with 200 C for NMC). It also ejects fewer solid fragments of battery when overheated — but more gas, Gupta said: "And that gas is often laden with both toxic and flammable products."
So, how do you stay safe?
Buy batteries with Canadian safety certifications such as CSA, cUL, cETL on the charger. Make sure you use the correct charger with your battery, even if another one fits in the charging port.
These are the kinds of certification marks you should look for on your battery charger, according to the Government of Canada lithium-ion battery safety website. (Health Canada)

Keep an eye on your charging battery and its environment. Charge your device or battery on a hard, non-flammable surface (not on a couch or bed), where you can see it. Gupta recommends not putting the device in the path that you would need to use to escape in case of a fire incident.
Know the danger signs of a damaged battery. They include feeling too hot, swelling, bad smells, gas or smoke.
There are some devices that can help identify these signs, such as:

items: TempAlert or other temperature-sensitive stickers that you can apply to the battery.
Heat detectors or alarms. Reader Adrian Hill of Crystal Beach, Ont., said he purchased one of these that he installed above the spot where he charges his e-bike.
A carbon monoxide detector. Gupta said many lithium batteries release carbon monoxide when overheated.

blocks.text: Know what to do if your battery overheats. Unplug it and get it to a safe, non-flammable place (such as outdoors, a sink or a bucket of sand) if possible. Don't try to charge it again, even if it cools, Giles says.
This is Call2Recycle's kit for dealing with damaged, defective or recalled lithium batteries at hazardous waste facilities. (Call2Recycle)

If it cools down, you can take it to a technician or hazardous waste disposal site. Do not put it in the trash. Call2Recycle has more detailed information on dealing with damaged, defective and recalled batteries.
If the battery continues getting hotter or releases gas or smoke, you're really in the danger zone.
"If you smell anything, that's bad," Gupta said. "You should leave and call the fire department."

Lithium batteries are around us everywhere and that's not going to change any time soon, he added. For the most part they're safe, but "it's important for people to be aware of the fact that they can fail and there are very simple things we can do that go a long way towards improving our personal safety."

articles.title: As a Nigerian, I thought Canadians had free health care. Then I became a pharmacist here
articles.summary: When Atai Okokon moved to Calgary from Nigeria, she was surprised to see that Canadians struggle to pay for medications in much the same way as Nigerians.

image.caption: As a pharmacist who worked in Nigeria and now calls Canada home, Atai Okokon did not expect to see her patients in Calgary struggle to pay for life-saving medications like she did in her home country. (Ola Ajayi)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person
When Atai Okokon moved to Calgary from Nigeria, she was surprised to see that Canadians struggle to pay for medications in much the same way as Nigerians.
As a patient and a pharmacist, I've found prescription drug costs can be a difficult pill to swallow
This First Person is the experience of Atai Okokon, who lives in Calgary. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
I asked the woman at the pharmacy counter how she would like to pay for her child’s asthma inhaler.
"Does my insurance no longer work?" she asked in a whisper, her voice shaky and unsure. "I was laid off and I am not sure how long my employer coverage would last."
I tried putting it through a second time.
"I am sorry, ma’am. The coverage has been terminated."
She brought out her credit card to pay. It was declined. She hesitated for a bit, turned out her purse to see if she had enough cash, but she was $2 short. The tears rolled freely down her cheeks.
Her son needed his medication, but she couldn't afford it.

It wasn't the first time I experienced this. I had seen it in Nigeria, where I had trained and worked as a pharmacist. I had witnessed people become bankrupt, and some die, because they could not afford life-saving medication. I had provided samples, paid for medicines from my meagre salary, offered less expensive alternatives and discontinued medications that may not have been necessary to lower their expenses.
But I did not expect to see it in Canada.
Okokon worked as a pharmacist in Nigeria before moving to Canada. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)

In 2012, I accepted a full scholarship to study global health at Oxford University in the U.K., leaving the counter for the classroom. It was there I first heard about the inverse care law — the concept that those with the most needs often have the least access to care. I assumed it mostly applied in “poorer” countries. I was surprised to learn that countries can spend so much on health care and yet their citizens struggle to pay for the services. North America featured prominently in these discussions and Canada stood out as a country that had made universal health care work.

Eight years after I graduated, I moved to Calgary. I had admired and loved Canada from afar and as a health-care professional, I was excited to practise in a country where I believed anyone — no matter how much they earned or where they lived — could access most health-care services without thinking of the cost.

items: Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada

blocks.text: I had a child after I moved to Canada and throughout my pregnancy, I did not spend a dime on routine tests, scans and specialist visits. I was unemployed but never worried about the cost of childbirth or what I would do if there were complications.
Okokon, left, with her mother Ekanem, in 2013 at a lunch at Oxford University for graduates and their families. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)

But that's also when I realized that getting medications was a different ball game. Outside the hospital, for the most part, medications are not free. I had terrible nausea in my first trimester. I woke up with it and, like a shadow, it stayed with me the whole day. The doctor prescribed medication but when I went to the pharmacy and heard the cost, I decided to find other ways to cope with the nausea.
“It will only last 12 weeks,” I told myself.
I was in the process of getting licensed as a pharmacist in Alberta and I did not want my husband, the sole provider at that time, to carry that extra financial burden.

items: His cancer drug costs $90,000/month. Doctors say it’s greed

blocks.text: That plan did not work. My nausea became worse and my husband bought a month’s worth of medication. I felt so guilty about the cost that I stretched it out, taking it only on the worst days, and said nothing to my husband. My doctor had also prescribed iron pills, as my levels were quite low, and a kind pharmacist gave me samples when I explained my financial situation.
Okokon with her family in Calgary in 2025. From left to right: her son Tomiwa, Okokon, her husband David and daughter, Toyosi. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)
One in five Canadians do not have drug insurance coverage and have to pay for their medication. I was one of them.

And so was the woman standing in front of me at the pharmacy counter. Her sniff jolted me back to reality. She had lost her job, and with it, her coverage. She now had to bear the cost of the inhaler her child needed. Luckily, we had some samples in the pharmacy and I gave her one.

She sighed in relief and through tears, told me the money she had with her would now go towards scraping together something for dinner. It was a déjà vu moment for me. I might as well have been behind the counter in Nigeria.
On the day Okokon took her citizenship oath in December 2024, her colleagues at her pharmacy in Calgary threw her a surprise party with cake and decorations. (Submitted by Atai Okokon)

Today, something similar happens on almost every shift. I find myself substituting, adapting, de-prescribing or troubleshooting insurance claims so that my patients can access the medicines they need. Just like I did in Nigeria.

I have experienced the health-care system of the country I now call home both as a patient and a practitioner and it’s made me realize a prescription is only a piece of paper when a patient cannot afford their medicines.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Atai Okokon is a pharmacist, who lives in Calgary with her husband and two children. Her work has appeared in The New York Times' Tiny Love Stories and Pharmacy Practice + Business Magazine.

articles.title: Storm warnings for Melbourne, Canberra, Sydney and Brisbane as cold front ‘packs a punch’
articles.summary:
BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into Sunday

  • Get our

blocks.text: Storm warnings are in place for multiple capital cities across Australia’s east and south-east as a severe weather front sweeps across the country.
Heavy rain, winds and thunderstorms are forecast to hit Melbourne and eastern Victoria throughout Saturday afternoon as a cold front meets warm, humid air.
The storm front is then expected to travel further east, impacting Canberra and inland NSW before reaching the east coast on Sunday, stretching as far as southern Queensland.
The Bureau of Meteorology warned of possible flash flooding in some areas and potentially destructive winds of over 125km/h that could bring down large trees or damage property.
Melbourne and parts of Victoria recorded moderate rainfall and some lightning on Saturday morning, with a more intense band of thunderstorms forecast into the afternoon.
“It’s this follow-up band of storms which could pack a punch,” BoM meteorologist Angus Hines said on Saturday.
The storms are expected to impact Melbourne, parts of Gippsland, the north-eastern ranges, and north-central Victoria, with damaging winds the greatest risk.
The risk area will extend further north through inland NSW into the evening – up to Queensland’s southern interior and along the NSW coast south of Sydney around Wollongong and the Illawarra.
The forecast in these areas includes possible damaging winds, heavy rainfall and large hailstones.

“Expecting some very active storms here a little bit later on in the day, mid to late afternoon for many of these areas, and potentially not until the evening hours by the time we’re looking at storms getting out towards the east coast,” Hines said.
The focus of concern will shift further north on Sunday, with heavy rain and storms around Brisbane during the afternoon and early evening.
after newsletter promotion

Severe thunderstorms were most likely for parts of the NSW mid-north coast, the northern rivers, parts of the tablelands and the Hunter region, with possible hail, heavy rainfall, flash flooding and destructive winds of more than 125km/h.
Areas that had recorded heightened rainfall in the past fortnight were also at risk of flash flooding, Hines said.
“If you do live through this area, tomorrow is definitely a day you’ll want to keep a watch on the radar to see if any big storms are headed your way,” he said.
A broader area of potential concern for Sunday stretches from Newcastle, north of Sydney, up to Gympie on the Sunshine Coast.
A severe wind warning is also in place across the mountains of northern Victoria and southern NSW, with wind gusts of more than 100km/h recorded on Saturday morning.

articles.title: Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
articles.summary: The Spanish PM is hit by a succession of crises just weeks before a snap general election.

blocks.text: The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.
From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.
On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.
The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.
Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.
He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.
In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.
The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.
In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.
Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.
The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid.
"They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop.
"I'm no judge... But these are the facts."
So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister.
"I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."
But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.
"This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.
An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails - very different to the latest collision.
But there is a similar impact.
"It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."
For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.
Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.
Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.
Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.
That's when Sánchez called an early election.
His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.
Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox.
"They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.
But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.
Suddenly, the tone has changed.

"They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."
There is also anger.

There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.
Here in Toledo, the mood is nervous.
"We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.
She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government.
"This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."
Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too.
"This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."
Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

articles.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
articles.summary: What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

image.caption: From childhood bullying to workplace discrimination, awkward names can influence how people are perceived and treatedImage: Dreamstime Demidovic/Dreamstime/IMAGO

blocks.text: As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.
"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."
The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?
"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."
Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.
This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.
How names influence first impressions

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."
"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.
What do Nigerians think of bullying?
Why some names attract negative judgments

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.
Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.
Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.
Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.
"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.
Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.
"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."
Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.
"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"
Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.
How humor helps people cope with embarrassing names
As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.
Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."
"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."
Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.
"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"
How an embarrassing name can also offer a sense of belonging
"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.
Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."
But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.
"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."
But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.
"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.
Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.
"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.
Superpower laughter — how humor makes us strong
Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."
But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.
Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.
For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.
"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

articles.title: India news: Amit Shah challenges Rahul Gandhi to debate vote theft in Parliament
articles.summary: Home Minister Amit Shah has challenged Rahul Gandhi to debate electoral irregularity allegations in parliament, ahead of a major opposition rally against the election chief in Delhi. DW has more.

image.caption: Amit Shah called the allegations against the Election Commission 'baseless' [FILE: May 8, 2026]Image: ANI Video Grab

blocks.text: October 31, 2026
Vote theft row: Shah challenges opposition as INDIA bloc prepares major protest

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Friday challenged opposition leaders Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav to discuss allegations of electoral irregularities in parliament, even as the opposition geared for a major rally against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar , according to media reports.

"I am ready to call a special session of Parliament to discuss vote theft allegations," Shah said, accusing the opposition of making baseless allegations against the Election Commission and staging protests while skirting parliamentary debate.
His remarks came as the opposition INDIA bloc prepared to hold a symbolic "public impeachment" of Kumar on Saturday, followed by a major rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on November 1.
Around 30 speakers from 21 opposition parties are expected to participate.

The opposition is demanding Kumar's resignation over his role in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the scrapping of the SIR, alleging that the exercise could disenfranchise voters and benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
In a call for the November 1 rally, Rahul Gandhi said "anyone who cares about democracy must come."
"The vote is yours. The fight is also yours," the Congress leader wrote on X.

Earlier, the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) also threw their weight behind the rally saying the movement would lend its support to any organization fighting for free and fair elections in India, including the opposition alliance.

articles.title: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara to expire amid US, Russia vetoes
articles.summary: The mandate of the UN peacekeeping force in Western Sahara will expire on October 31. The UN Security Council could not agree on a resolution to extend the mission.

image.caption: Friday's failed US draft resolution would have rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination.Image: FADEL SENNA/AFP

blocks.text: The fate of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has been left in a limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed each other's draft resolutions on extending the mission that is over three decades long — just one day before the mandate expires.

The peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to oversee a settlement plan and ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front in a territorial dispute spanning half a century.
Morocco considers Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, as its territory,
The Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria and represents the indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
US and Russia wield vetoes

On Friday, the US tabled a draft resolution at the UN Security Council (UNSC) that would have extended the mandate for one year, while making a Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara the only basis for negotiations to settle the conflict, and cutting the mission's military component.
Last year, the UNSC backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.

Friday's failed US draft resolution would have gone further and rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination.
The US proposal was vetoed by Russia, which slammed it as a "unilateral approach." A total of 11 of the 15 UNSC members voted in its favor and three abstained.
"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, said.
"The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of ⁠the draft," ​he added.
The US, with its own veto, then blocked a Russian draft that proposed renewing the mission's mandate for another year while preserving the same terms as before.

"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," the US representative to the United Nations, Michael Waltz, said after the vote.
Western Sahara: Caught between sovereignty and struggle
How did Morocco and the Polisario Front react?

Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the peacekeeping mission and said that this "should mark the end of the Security Council's involvement and the removal of this issue from its agenda."

The Polisario Front's UN representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing the US resolution that he said "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence."

articles.title: Trump's tariffs could shutter this Canadian town - its residents are fighting to save it
articles.summary: A century-old paper mill in Témiscaming, Quebec is indefinitely closed after the US imposed 50% tariffs on its products, putting hundreds out of work.

blocks.text: "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec town
ByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and Nadine YousifSenior Canada reporter
As you cross the Ottawa river into Témiscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon.

The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country.
Most of the mill‘s 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief.
For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life.

She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year.
"It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack".
In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period".
Property values in Témiscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town.
There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out.
"If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers.
"There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Jessica Murphy
The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.

At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth.

But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of Témiscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive.

"If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,” says Stéphane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill.

That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people.

The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it.
They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France.
The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017.
"We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall.
But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support.

Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge.
In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Nadine Yousif
Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.
Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada".
He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free.
And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken".
"We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back."
Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos.

This month, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure.
Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024.

Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; £4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said.

Sébastien Lemire, the elected MP for Témiscaming from the Bloc Québécois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly.
A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas.
It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets.

On the Témiscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry.

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied/Stéphane Lefebvre
Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry.
In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes.
Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs.

The Témiscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US.
Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in Témiscaming.
Frank Dottori has been through all of this before.

Now in his 80s and retired in Témiscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO.
Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support.
But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma.
Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold.
"Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they if they organise themselves," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship

blocks.text: Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship
It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term.

Many workers in Témiscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump — whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls — to ease some of his tariffs on Canada.
"We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too."

There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at Témiscaming's mill, however.
Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult.
In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens.
"We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."

articles.title: Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms
articles.summary:
The prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda

  • Get our

blocks.text: As “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker for Anthony Albanese amid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said.
But a likely interest rate hike triggered by higher-than-expected inflation while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder.
Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday.
He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting.

The discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies over grant funding and pressures on inflation, according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University.
“It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said.
“He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot.
“There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.”
Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.
It would be the fifth interest rate hike in 2026 and a challenging situation for the government to navigate, amid continuing cost-of-living pressures.

Albanese emphasised the value of attending Chogm before his departure on Saturday morning. In a crowded international calendar, the Commonwealth is occasionally dismissed as irrelevant, an anachronistic relic of a former imperial era.
“The Commonwealth heads of government meeting is an important forum,” Albanese said.
“[It provides] an opportunity to work with some of our closest partners on shared challenges, including climate change, the preservation of our oceans, trade and investment and the rise of AI.”
after newsletter promotion
The issue of historical slavery, and its ongoing legacy, is likely to be a key point of contention at Chogm.
Burnham, writing in the Guardian, said having “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future” was the right thing to do.
“Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”
He called the transatlantic slave trade a “brutal and barbaric violation” of people “treated as property and worked to their deaths”.
“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he wrote.
Caribbean nations have made renewed calls for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit, and for reparations, as the King toured the Caribbean.

Burnham said: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.” But he said he did not believe reparations for slavery was the “right answer”.
Australia would not be a bystander to any debate about slavery and the slave trade.

Across the 19th and early 20th centuries, Australian agriculture relied heavily on “blackbirding”: the use of coercion, trickery, bribery and kidnapping to bring more than 60,000 Pacific Islanders to work as indentured labourers in Australia, primarily on Queensland’s sugar and cotton plantations.
The Chogm meeting will kick off a busy end to the year overseas for Albanese, with international summits in Turkey, the Philippines, China and the US in coming weeks.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is currently in Atlanta, Georgia for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting.
